questions.question: An ED nurse disposing of a blood-draw needle was stuck by a needle protruding from a sharps container that had been jammed past capacity; about five months later she was diagnosed with both HIV and hepatitis C. What sharps practice would have prevented this injury?
choices: Push protruding needles down into the container with a gloved hand before adding more sharps.
Empty overfilled containers into a larger bin so they can keep being used.
Recap every needle before disposal so nothing can protrude from the container.
Never force a sharp into a full container; replace containers at the fill line and report overfilled ones.
questions.explanation: She was injured by someone else's careless disposal; containers must be replaced at the fill line, never forced.

questions.question: Assessment in Action: Because your partner did not use standard precautions, he has potentially been exposed to an infectious disease. What should he do?
choices: Ignore it because the risk of contamination is small.
Report it to the hospital staff so they can isolate the patient.
Report it to the infection control officer.
Sanitize any equipment that was in contact with the patient.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed answer key.

questions.question: What does the term "sharps safety" mean?
choices: Cleaning and disinfecting the ambulance and its equipment after a call, including allowing disinfected surfaces to air dry unless otherwise indicated in the product directions, so the unit is safe for the next patient.
Inflammation of the liver, usually caused by a viral infection, that causes fever, loss of appetite, nausea, intestinal upset, and often jaundice.
Handling needles and other sharps carefully and disposing of them properly; careless handling of sharps is the usual route by which HIV and hepatitis are spread in health care settings.

A sexually transmitted infectious disease caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum; unlike many infections, it confers no protection from reinfection after exposure, so a treated person can catch it again.
questions.explanation: sharps safety: Handling needles and other sharps carefully and disposing of them properly; careless handling of sharps is the usual route by which HIV and hepatitis are spread in health care settings.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A situation in which a person has had contact with blood, body fluids, tissues, or airborne particles and has the potential to develop a disease.
questions.explanation: exposure: A situation in which a person has had contact with blood, body fluids, tissues, or airborne particles and has the potential to develop a disease.

questions.question: At a crash scene, blood and fluids may splash while you control bleeding and clear an airway. What should you put on to protect your eyes, instead of relying on regular glasses?
questions.explanation: Proper rated protection, such as goggles or a face shield, covers the sides regular glasses leave open.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: What airborne bacterial disease is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spreads when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and is indicated by a positive skin test showing exposure to the bacterium.
questions.explanation: tuberculosis: What airborne bacterial disease is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spreads when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and is indicated by a positive skin test showing exposure to the bacterium.

questions.question: During a multi-casualty drill, a paramedic notices she feels energized and clear-headed under the time pressure, and her triage times are her fastest ever. What term describes this positive stress response?
questions.explanation: The pressure acted as a benefit, sharpening her work; a beneficial response to a stressor is eustress.

questions.question: After transporting a patient with bloody vomiting, you wipe down the stretcher and bench with disinfectant and immediately dry everything with a towel so the unit looks ready. What step of ambulance decontamination did you defeat?
questions.explanation: Disinfectants need their full contact time; surfaces should be allowed to air dry unless the product directions say otherwise.

questions.question: After removing your gloves following a call with a patient who has influenza, your hands look clean, so you head straight to the next call. What should you have done first?
choices: putting on a new pair of gloves
questions.explanation: Gloves can leak or tear and hands are contaminated during glove removal, so hand washing is required after every patient contact.

questions.question: After the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing, adults who watched 6 or more hours of bombing coverage per day were nine times more likely to report high acute stress than people with minimal exposure — higher even than many who were at the scene. What should a responder who worked the incident do?
choices: Media exposure cannot cause real stress reactions, so viewing habits after a call do not matter.
Watch coverage repeatedly until the images stop bothering you, since desensitization is the fastest cure.
Only direct exposure at the scene counts, so off-duty viewing is a safe way to process the event.
Limit exposure to graphic coverage of the incident, because repeated viewing can intensify your own acute stress reaction.
questions.explanation: Limit your exposure to graphic coverage of an incident you worked; repeated viewing can intensify your own acute stress reaction.

questions.question: On Christmas Eve 2012 in Webster, New York, a man set his house and car on fire to lure responders, then fired on arriving firefighters from a hidden earthen berm across the street, killing two. What should crews do at a suspicious fire like this?
choices: Stage out of sight, scan for a hidden shooter, and use objects that block the shooter's view before committing to the scene.
Move straight to the fire and begin suppression, since a working structure fire leaves no time to stage.
Approach on foot in the open so the suspect can clearly see that responders are unarmed.
Park the ambulance directly in front of the burning house to light the scene for police.
questions.explanation: Stage out of sight at any suspicious fire and scan for a hidden shooter before committing to the scene.

questions.question: A paramedic supervisor replaced fentanyl in ambulance vials with saline and falsified the narcotics logs; an audit later found 26 of 28 fentanyl vials tampered with, and field crews had noticed the drug sometimes seemed ineffective at relieving pain. When crews notice that a narcotic seems ineffective, seals look broken, or log counts do not match, what should they do?
choices: Assume the pharmacy supplied a weak batch and keep using the remaining vials until the next scheduled audit.
Mention it to coworkers informally but wait for a patient complaint before filing any report.
Quietly discard the suspect vials and restock the narcotics box so the unit stays in service.
Treat ineffective narcotics, broken seals, and log discrepancies as red flags and report them immediately.
questions.explanation: Ineffective narcotics, broken seals, and log discrepancies are red flags for diversion and must be reported immediately.

questions.question: Two years after working a mass-casualty crash, an EMT notices her symptoms peaked only recently even though she functioned well at first. What is this pattern called?
questions.explanation: A reaction that emerges or peaks well after the stressful situation is a delayed stress reaction.

questions.question: A patient feels completely healthy, but lab tests show the hepatitis C virus is active in his liver. Even with no signs or symptoms, this invasion of a host by an organism is called what?
questions.explanation: The definition covers invasion with or without signs or symptoms of disease.

questions.question: What does the term "infection control" mean?
choices: Procedures to reduce transmission of infection among patients and health care personnel.
Handling needles and other sharps carefully and disposing of them properly; careless handling of sharps is the usual route by which HIV and hepatitis are spread in health care settings.

A sexually transmitted infectious disease caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum; unlike many infections, it confers no protection from reinfection after exposure, so a treated person can catch it again.
Pathogenic microorganisms that are present in human blood and can cause disease in humans. These pathogens include, but are not limited to, hepatitis B virus and human immunodeficiency virus.
questions.explanation: infection control: Procedures to reduce transmission of infection among patients and health care personnel.

questions.question: Harvard researcher Alison Wood Brooks studied karaoke singing, public speaking, and math performance in 2014. Participants who said 'I am excited' before performing did better than those who tried to calm down. What technique does this case illustrate for an EMT facing a high-pressure call?
choices: Fight to calm down first, because lowering arousal is the only proven way to perform well under pressure.
Avoid the high-pressure assignment until the anxiety fades on its own over time.
Relabel the anxiety as excitement, since both are high-arousal states and the relabel converts stress into a beneficial response.
Treat the anxiety as a warning sign of an acute stress reaction that requires removal from the call.
questions.explanation: Saying 'I am excited' instead of fighting to calm down is an evidence-based way to make stress work for you.

questions.question: A station captain tells a new EMT, 'Go out with me and I will put you on the day shift you want; say no and you stay on nights.' What type of sexual harassment is this?
questions.explanation: A supervisor tied a sexual favor to a shift benefit.

questions.question: A nursing home calls because six residents on one wing developed the same stomach virus over two days after sharing a dining room. The facility is asking how it moved between residents who never left the building. What kind of disease are they dealing with?
questions.explanation: A communicable disease passes between people, so shared air, surfaces, and close contact in one wing can move it from resident to resident.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (4-year-old girl in cardiac arrest): What stage of the grieving process is the mother experiencing?
choices: Anger, the second stage of the Kübler-Ross grief process (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance). Anger directed at EMS is a normal reaction to loss, not personal.
Denial, the first stage of the Kübler-Ross grief process (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance). Her yelling is an attempt to reject what is happening.
Bargaining, the third stage of the Kübler-Ross grief process (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance). She is trying to negotiate for her daughter's life.
Depression, the fourth stage of the Kübler-Ross grief process (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance). Her crying shows she has accepted the likely outcome.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.

questions.question: Your patient is a teenager whose body the influenza virus has invaded and is now producing fever and aches. In infection terms, what is the patient in relation to the virus?
questions.explanation: The patient is the individual attacked by the infecting agent, which is the definition of a host.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The organism or individual that is attacked by the infecting agent.
questions.explanation: host: The organism or individual that is attacked by the infecting agent.

questions.question: Police tell you to wait behind a wooden fence, out of the suspect's line of sight, until the scene is secure. The fence hides you but could not stop a bullet. This is an example of what?
questions.explanation: An object used only to block someone's view of you is concealment, not cover.

questions.question: What does the term "vehicle stabilization" mean?
choices: Securing a crashed vehicle with cribbing, struts, or other supports so it cannot move, shift, or roll; it must be done to ensure the vehicle is stable before attempting to access a patient trapped inside.
A situation in which a person has had contact with blood, body fluids, tissues, or airborne particles and has the potential to develop a disease.
The simplest, yet most effective, method of preventing the spread of infectious disease: washing the hands in between patient contacts.
A process that confronts the responses to critical incidents and defuses them, directing the emergency services personnel toward physical and emotional equilibrium.
questions.explanation: vehicle stabilization: Securing a crashed vehicle with cribbing, struts, or other supports so it cannot move, shift, or roll; it must be done to ensure the vehicle is stable before attempting to access a patient trapped inside.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A beneficial response to a stressor.
questions.explanation: eustress: A beneficial response to a stressor.

questions.question: A sedan sits nose-down in a ditch on a slope, rocking slightly whenever rescuers lean on it. Before cutting tools come out, the crew chief orders cribbing and struts placed at four points. What safety step is she enforcing?
questions.explanation: Ensuring the vehicle is stable before attempting access prevents movement that can crush rescuers or worsen the patient's injuries.

questions.question: Dispatch sends you to a correctional facility for a man with fever, fatigue, and a chronic cough. Other inmates were recently diagnosed after sharing the same dormitory air for weeks. What airborne bacterial disease is most concerning here?
questions.explanation: It spreads through airborne droplets in crowded, shared-air settings like dormitories and shelters.

questions.question: A 21-year-old pregnant woman was treated for syphilis in her first trimester and her VDRL titers fell as expected, but at week 39 the titer rose again and clinicians diagnosed reinfection; her newborn tested positive and was treated for congenital syphilis. What does this case teach about a history of treated syphilis?
choices: A history of treated syphilis never rules out syphilis; reinfection can occur even later in the same pregnancy, so retesting matters.
Treatment in the first trimester always protects the newborn for the rest of the pregnancy.
Newborn testing is unnecessary when the mother completed syphilis treatment earlier in pregnancy.
A falling VDRL titer after treatment means the patient is immune from then on.
questions.explanation: Treatment early in pregnancy did not protect her or her baby, because syphilis reinfection later in the same pregnancy is a real event.

questions.question: What does the term "contamination" mean?
choices: The body's ability to protect itself from acquiring a disease.
A situation in which a person has had contact with blood, body fluids, tissues, or airborne particles and has the potential to develop a disease.
The presence of infectious organisms on or in objects such as dressings, water, food, needles, wounds, or a patient's body.
The contamination of food or water with an organism that can cause disease.
questions.explanation: contamination: The presence of infectious organisms on or in objects such as dressings, water, food, needles, wounds, or a patient's body.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The contamination of food or water with an organism that can cause disease.
questions.explanation: foodborne transmission: The contamination of food or water with an organism that can cause disease.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Reactions to stress that occur during a stressful situation.
questions.explanation: acute stress reactions: Reactions to stress that occur during a stressful situation.

questions.question: A new EMT is nervous before his first solo shift. Instead of dreading it, he uses the nerves to double-check his gear, review protocols, and arrive early. What type of stress response is he showing?
questions.explanation: His stress response produced preparation and better performance, a beneficial outcome, so it is eustress rather than distress.

questions.question: A measles outbreak in Gaines County, Texas in 2025 grew to 762 confirmed cases, with 99 people hospitalized and 2 children dead, as the virus spread person to person through the air in undervaccinated communities. You are dispatched to a child with a suspected measles rash and fever. What precaution does this case call for?
choices: No special precautions are needed as long as the patient's rash is covered with a blanket.
Wear a surgical mask only during the physical exam, then remove it for the ride to the hospital.
Use contact precautions only, since measles spreads mainly through contaminated surfaces.
Use airborne precautions and wear an N95 or respirator for any suspected measles patient.
questions.explanation: Measles is among the most contagious airborne diseases, so suspected cases require airborne precautions and a respirator.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The federal regulatory compliance agency that develops, publishes, and enforces guidelines concerning employee safety.
questions.explanation: Occupational Safety and Health Administration: The federal regulatory compliance agency that develops, publishes, and enforces guidelines concerning employee safety.

questions.question: A hiker in Connecticut finds a deer tick attached to his leg. A week later he develops a bull's-eye rash and swollen knees, and testing shows a bacterial infection carried by the tick. By what method was this organism spread?
questions.explanation: The tick is an animal that carried the organism to the patient, which is exactly how vector-borne spread works.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Prolonged or excessive stress.
questions.explanation: cumulative stress reactions: Prolonged or excessive stress.

questions.question: At a Las Vegas endoscopy clinic in 2008, nurse anesthetists reused syringes and contaminated single-dose propofol vials, spreading hepatitis C to later patients and forcing tens of thousands of former patients to be notified for testing. What rule would have prevented this?
choices: One needle, one syringe, one time: never re-enter a vial with used equipment.
A syringe can be reused on the same vial as long as the needle is wiped with alcohol first.
Reusing a syringe is acceptable when the first patient has no known infectious disease.
Single-dose vials may be shared between patients if everyone receives the same medication.
questions.explanation: One reused syringe turned a shared vial into a contaminated vehicle for every patient after it.

questions.question: You crouch behind a row of tall hedges while approaching a patient so an aggressive bystander cannot spot you. What are you using?
questions.explanation: The hedges limit the bystander's ability to see you, which is the definition of concealment.

questions.question: After a needlestick, your service's designated officer tells you the biggest long-term risk is a bloodborne virus that attacks the liver and can cause chronic liver disease. Which condition is he describing?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B and C are bloodborne viruses whose main target organ is the liver.

questions.question: After a needlestick, a paramedic completes an incident report, gets baseline blood tests, and is offered follow-up care. This whole process is triggered by which event?
questions.explanation: The needlestick created contact with blood and a potential for disease, which is an exposure.

questions.question: The SNIPS study surveyed 1,112 US EMS providers in 2021 and found that almost 90% screened positive for burnout, with about 41.5% reporting mental health concerns at some point in their EMS careers; EMTs and women screened positive at higher rates than paramedics and men. How should an EMT view these findings?
choices: Assume burnout only affects new providers, so experienced EMTs do not need to monitor themselves.
Treat a positive burnout screening as a personal weakness that should be hidden from supervisors and partners.
Screen yourself honestly for burnout signs; at these rates it is an occupational hazard to manage, not a personal failure.
Wait until symptoms disappear on their own, since burnout screening has no value for working crews.
questions.explanation: With nearly 90% of surveyed EMS providers screening positive, burnout is an occupational hazard to manage, not a personal failure.

questions.question: A nebulizer treatment is running on a pneumonia patient and fine mist fills the back of the unit. What kind of procedure is nebulization classified as?
questions.explanation: Nebulizers generate aerosols that can carry pathogens through the air.

questions.question: What does the term "Occupational Safety and Health Administration" mean?
choices: The tactical use of an impenetrable barrier for protection.

The formal, structured group debriefing held 24 to 72 hours after a critical incident, as part of critical incident stress management (CISM), in which the responders involved discuss the incident and their reactions to it.
The federal regulatory compliance agency that develops, publishes, and enforces guidelines concerning employee safety.
Inflammation of the liver, usually caused by a viral infection, that causes fever, loss of appetite, nausea, intestinal upset, and often jaundice.
questions.explanation: Occupational Safety and Health Administration: The federal regulatory compliance agency that develops, publishes, and enforces guidelines concerning employee safety.

questions.question: In 1976, 221 attendees of an American Legion convention at a Philadelphia hotel fell ill with pneumonia and 34 died. CDC investigator Joseph McDade identified a previously unknown bacterium, Legionella pneumophila, traced to the hotel's cooling tower. What is the main lesson of this investigation for an EMT?
choices: Respiratory illness clusters should be attributed to weather changes unless a pathogen is confirmed.
Treat unexplained clusters of respiratory illness as infectious until proven otherwise.
Only illnesses with a known cause require the crew to wear respiratory protection.
Clusters of pneumonia at one building are usually caused by food poisoning and need no precautions.
questions.explanation: A brand-new pathogen caused the outbreak before anyone knew it existed, so unexplained illness clusters must be treated as infectious.

questions.question: A neighboring agency's peer-support team offers pre-incident stress education, on-scene support during a long recovery operation, and one-on-one follow-ups afterward. Together, these services make up what?
questions.explanation: Pre-incident education, on-scene support, defusing, debriefing, and follow-up are all parts of the CISM process.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (4-year-old girl in cardiac arrest): How should you respond to the mother?
choices: Use a calm, professional, compassionate manner. Be honest but do not give false hope. Explain what you are doing in simple terms, allow the mother to stay with the child if it is safe, use active listening, acknowledge her feelings, avoid medical jargon, and use a team member to support her if possible.
Ask her to leave the room immediately, because family members are never permitted to watch a resuscitation attempt.
Reassure her that her daughter will be fine so she stays calm, and avoid explaining details that might upset her further.
Explain the situation using precise medical terminology so she understands exactly how serious the child's condition is.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.

questions.question: A tick picks up the Lyme disease bacterium while feeding on an infected white-footed mouse, then later bites a hiker. In the first part of that chain, what role does the mouse play for the bacterium?
questions.explanation: The mouse is the organism the infecting agent lives in and attacks, which makes it the host.

questions.question: At an assisted-living facility, eight residents developed acute hepatitis B and six died; every case was among the residents staff helped with blood glucose monitoring, and investigators found fingerstick devices and glucose meters shared without cleaning between residents. When you assist with glucose checks on a call, what should you do?
choices: Share the meter between residents but change only the test strip each time.
Never share fingerstick devices, and disinfect blood glucose meters between patients, because blood glucose equipment is blood equipment.
Use the shared fingerstick device as long as you wipe it with an alcohol prep first.
Skip disinfecting the meter when the resident has no known bloodborne infection.
questions.explanation: Shared blood glucose equipment spreads hepatitis B; never share fingerstick devices and disinfect meters between patients.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A negative response to a stressor.
questions.explanation: distress: A negative response to a stressor.

questions.question: In Toronto in 2003, healthcare workers were infected with SARS after intubating a SARS patient, and 72% of the city's SARS cases were healthcare-related. What protection does this case require for airway procedures on respiratory patients?
choices: A surgical mask alone is enough, since intubation does not expose the crew to aerosols.
Gloves are the key protection during intubation because the risk is mainly from touching the patient.
Only the person holding the laryngoscope needs protection; everyone else in the room is safe.
Wear a fit-tested respirator and eye protection for every intubation of a respiratory patient.
questions.explanation: Intubation aerosolizes the virus into the room, so the whole team needs a respirator and eye protection.

questions.question: A sedan sat on a street with about a 15-degree grade with the driver trapped inside. Focused on the extrication, the crew began running a hydraulic tool on the door without stabilizing the vehicle, and the force rolled the car forward, with the patient inside, toward other fire units; a crewmember stopped it with a cribbing block under the rear tire and no one was injured. What rule does this near-miss establish?
choices: Stabilize the vehicle only after extrication is underway and movement is noticed.
Chock and crib on arrival, even on 'routine' crashes; slopes turn small tool forces into rolling vehicles.
Rely on the parking brake and transmission to hold a vehicle on a grade during extrication.
Have one rescuer brace the car by hand while the tools are running.
questions.explanation: An unstabilized vehicle on a grade moved under tool pressure; chocking and cribbing on arrival prevents the second incident.

questions.question: During the spring 2020 COVID-19 peak, FDNY EMS handled a record of more than 6,500 calls in a single day. Three FDNY EMS workers died by suicide within a three-month period, calls to the department's counseling hotline rose 36%, and the department more than doubled its EMS peer counselors from 20 to 45 as crews described exhaustion and dread. What does this case show EMTs about getting help?
choices: A busy service should cut peer counselor positions first, since high call volume leaves no time to use them.
Counseling resources are meant for patients' families, not for EMS providers themselves.
Use peer support and counseling resources early; this case shows what happens to a whole service when burnout goes unaddressed.
Peer support should be used only after a provider has already decided to leave the profession.
questions.explanation: FDNY's experience shows burnout can overwhelm an entire service, so peer support and counseling should be used early, before it goes unaddressed.

questions.question: Navigate Case Study (EMT with delayed stress after a school bus MCI): What kinds of situations will you now be more aware of as having a higher level of stress for you and your coworkers?
choices: Calls are stressful mainly when the weather is bad or the drive is long; the type of patient and the outcome of the call matter very little.
Routine, low-acuity calls such as minor sprains and general weakness carry the highest stress because they are the most common calls in EMS.
Administrative tasks such as restocking the ambulance and completing paperwork are the highest-stress situations for most EMTs and their coworkers.

Calls involving seriously ill or injured children, especially a child's death, and mass-casualty incidents carry the highest stress. Other high-stress calls include patients who resemble a family member, the death or serious injury of a coworker, violent scenes, and repeated exposure to disturbing calls over time.
questions.explanation: Answer written from the chapter (no printed key).

questions.question: Two to three weeks after September 11, 2001, researchers surveyed 90 World Trade Center disaster workers and found nearly 15% had probable acute stress disorder and more than half of tobacco users had increased their smoking. What does this show about acute stress reactions?
choices: Acute stress reactions are common and measurable in the first weeks after a mass-casualty event, and they are not a sign of weakness.
Stress reactions that appear within weeks of an event are harmless and never change daily behavior.
Acute stress reactions are rare in trained responders and usually indicate poor fitness for the job.
Only responders who were physically injured at a disaster are at risk for acute stress reactions.
questions.explanation: Acute stress reactions are common and measurable in the first weeks after a mass-casualty event, not a sign of weakness.

questions.question: A 40-year-old fire captain fell repeatedly from a personal watercraft during surf rescue training in about 47 degree F water. He wore a dry suit over a jumpsuit, but his hood and thin gloves were not waterproof and gave minimal thermal protection once wet; he died two days later from complications involving hypothermia. What failed in his clothing system?
choices: The jumpsuit under the dry suit was the problem, because layering under a dry suit traps cold water.
The dry suit itself failed, showing that dry suits should not be used for surf rescue training.
Nothing about the clothing failed; the outcome was caused only by the length of the swim.
The system failed at its weakest points, so every part of a cold-water clothing system, including gloves and hood, must be waterproof and insulated before training or response.
questions.explanation: Cold-weather layers only preserve heat if every layer, including hood and gloves, stays protective when wet.

questions.question: During the 1997 North Hollywood shootout, rifle rounds from two armored bank robbers penetrated patrol-car sheet metal, wounding officers who were using cars for protection. On a shooting scene, what does this case teach about protecting yourself?
choices: Stay in the open where you can see the shooter rather than hiding behind any barrier.
Use bushes and wooden fences, which stop bullets as effectively as concrete.
Crouch behind the ambulance door, since vehicle sheet metal reliably stops rifle rounds.
Put engine blocks, concrete, or earth between you and the threat, not sheet metal.
questions.explanation: Car doors are concealment, not cover; only bullet-stopping barriers like engine blocks and concrete protect against rifle fire.

questions.question: What does the term "pathogen" mean?
choices: A microorganism that is capable of causing disease in a susceptible host.
The individual in the department who is charged with the responsibility of managing exposures and infection control.
Pathogenic microorganisms that are present in human blood and can cause disease in humans. These pathogens include, but are not limited to, hepatitis B virus and human immunodeficiency virus.

The misuse of drugs or alcohol by a provider, on or off duty, that endangers the provider, coworkers, and patients; among EMS personnel, its most serious consequence is substandard or inappropriate patient care.
questions.explanation: pathogen: A microorganism that is capable of causing disease in a susceptible host.

questions.question: In 2012, a Tennessee clinician reported a rare fungal meningitis case in a patient who had received an epidural steroid injection; the report triggered a multistate investigation that traced the infections to contaminated medication lots from one compounding pharmacy, and roughly 14,000 patients were notified. What should providers take from this case?
choices: Wait until at least ten similar cases appear locally before reporting anything to public health.
Report unusual post-treatment infections promptly; one report to public health can protect thousands of patients.
Keep the report inside your own agency to avoid alarming the public unnecessarily.
Report the infection only to the medication manufacturer rather than to public health officials.
questions.explanation: One prompt report to public health can trigger an investigation that protects thousands of patients.
questions.topic: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

questions.question: Your patient picked up hepatitis A after eating raw scallops later traced to a contaminated import shipment. What term covers this foodborne route of spread?
questions.explanation: Disease spread by a vehicle such as food is one route of transmission.

questions.question: A new EMT asks why the service has written rules for glove use, sharps containers, and cleaning the rig. The officer explains the rules exist to cut the spread of disease between patients and crews. What are these rules called?
questions.explanation: Standardized steps that reduce infection transmission are infection control procedures.

questions.question: Assessment in Action: What standard precautions should your partner have taken with this patient?
questions.explanation: From the book's printed answer key.

questions.question: Two days after a school bus rollover with several seriously injured children, your agency brings the crews who responded together for a formal, led group session to talk through the call and their reactions. What is this session called?
questions.explanation: A formal group debriefing held 24-72 hours after a critical incident is a CISD, part of CISM.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The active pursuit of a state of good health.
questions.explanation: wellness: The active pursuit of a state of good health.

questions.question: What does the term "indirect contact" mean?
choices: Exposure or transmission of disease from one person to another by contact with a contaminated object.
The individual in the department who is charged with the responsibility of managing exposures and infection control.
The body's ability to protect itself from acquiring a disease.
The presence of infectious organisms on or in objects such as dressings, water, food, needles, wounds, or a patient's body.
questions.explanation: indirect contact: Exposure or transmission of disease from one person to another by contact with a contaminated object.

questions.question: David Vetter, born in 1971 with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), lived in a sterile isolator at Texas Children's Hospital because his immune system could not fight infection; germ-free isolation was the only protection available to him. What does his case mean for EMTs caring for an immunocompromised patient?
choices: Standard precautions can be relaxed, because a patient kept in isolation is already protected from germs.
Providers need no protective equipment, since the patient's condition is genetic rather than contagious to the crew.
Strict infection control around an immunocompromised patient is not optional, because the patient has no immune safety net.
The patient's own antibodies will handle minor exposures, so brief lapses in technique carry little risk.
questions.explanation: Immunocompromised patients have no safety net; strict infection control around them is not optional.

questions.question: A hospital diagnoses a transported patient with meningitis two days after the call and must notify the transporting EMS agency. Under the Ryan White notification process, the hospital communicates with which person at the agency?
questions.explanation: The designated officer is the department's official point of contact for exposure notification and infection control.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: What are the hazards at a structure fire that include possible building collapse, high heat, smoke and toxic gases, and oxygen-deficient air, and that require EMTs to stage at a safe distance and stay clear until the fire department declares the scene safe.
questions.explanation: structural fire hazards: What are the hazards at a structure fire that include possible building collapse, high heat, smoke and toxic gases, and oxygen-deficient air, and that require EMTs to stage at a safe distance and stay clear until the fire department declares the scene safe.

questions.question: A nursing home resident develops fever, dark urine, and yellowing of the skin two months after a fingerstick procedure. Lab work points to a viral liver infection. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fever plus jaundice after a blood exposure fits hepatitis, an inflammation of the liver.

questions.question: Assessment in Action: If your partner becomes infected with this patient’s illness, what type of transmission would this occur through?
questions.explanation: From the book's printed answer key.

questions.question: After years of night shifts and rising call volume, a medic tells his partner, 'I just don't care anymore, and I'm not the clinician I was.' He is tired all the time and his performance reviews have slipped. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Long-term job stress has produced the three defining features: exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced performance.

questions.question: Your service issues gowns, gloves, and fit-tested respirators for calls involving a patient with suspected tuberculosis. What category of safety equipment do these items belong to?
questions.explanation: Each item is protective equipment that blocks exposure to a pathogen or hazardous material, the definition of PPE.

questions.question: After a nurse in Dallas caught Ebola from a patient in 2014, CDC required no exposed skin and a trained observer for donning and doffing PPE. Which CDC framework was being tightened?
questions.explanation: The PPE, hand hygiene, and exposure rules for all patient care sit inside standard precautions.

questions.question: Before starting an IV on a combative, vomiting patient, your partner puts on rated safety glasses with side shields. What is this PPE called?
questions.explanation: Rated eyewear with side protection blocks fluid reaching the eye's mucous membranes.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A process that confronts the responses to critical incidents and defuses them, directing the emergency services personnel toward physical and emotional equilibrium.
questions.explanation: critical incident stress management: A process that confronts the responses to critical incidents and defuses them, directing the emergency services personnel toward physical and emotional equilibrium.

questions.question: A diabetic patient has a foot wound, but the redness, swelling, and fever come from bacteria invading and multiplying in the tissue rather than from the injury itself. What type of medical condition has developed in the wound?
questions.explanation: Bacteria growing and spreading within the body's tissues created a new condition, which is an infectious disease.

questions.question: What does the term "host" mean?
choices: The spread of an organism via droplets or dust.
The organism or individual that is attacked by the infecting agent.
The way in which an infectious disease is spread: contact, airborne, by vehicles, or by vectors.
The capacity of an individual to cope with and recover from distress.
questions.explanation: host: The organism or individual that is attacked by the infecting agent.

questions.question: In 2001, an anthrax letter sent to Senator Daschle passed through Washington, DC's Brentwood mail facility before it was opened. Postal workers Thomas Morris Jr. and Joseph Curseen Jr. died of inhalation anthrax without ever opening the letter, and nearly 1,900 employees received full 60-day antibiotic courses. What does this case teach about an exposure?
choices: An exposure does not require symptoms — report it the same shift and follow the follow-up plan.
Only people who directly handled the letter need testing or preventive treatment.
An exposure is only official once a laboratory confirms the person is infected.
Workers without symptoms should wait to see if they get sick before reporting anything.
questions.explanation: The Brentwood workers were exposed without being patients at first, and exposure alone triggered testing, antibiotics, and monitoring.

questions.question: After completing his hepatitis B vaccine series and a titer showing antibodies, a paramedic is told his body can now defend itself against hepatitis B. What state has he achieved against that disease?
questions.explanation: Vaccination gave his body the ability to protect itself from acquiring hepatitis B, so he is immune to it.

questions.question: A nursing-home patient tells you his TB skin test was positive last year but he never developed symptoms or took treatment. Today he has a new persistent cough. Your crew treats this as possible active disease and uses airborne precautions. What infection does a positive skin test show exposure to?
questions.explanation: A positive skin test shows exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis; latent infection can later become active disease.

questions.question: In 2011, Listeria monocytogenes on whole cantaloupes from Jensen Farms in Colorado infected 147 people in 28 states. Thirty-three people died, most of them elderly, and one pregnant patient miscarriage. CDC called it the deadliest US foodborne outbreak in decades. What should EMTs keep in mind from this case?
choices: Listeriosis only causes mild stomach upset and never affects pregnant patients.
Produce cannot transmit disease, so fever in an elderly patient after eating melon is unrelated to food.
Elderly and pregnant patients with fever and confusion after suspect food should have listeriosis considered, since foodborne illness can be deadly in these groups.
Foodborne outbreaks stay local, so a nationally distributed product is not a concern for EMS.
questions.explanation: A single contaminated food item distributed nationally shows how far foodborne transmission can reach before it is detected.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Pathogenic microorganisms that are present in human blood and can cause disease in humans. These pathogens include, but are not limited to, hepatitis B virus and human immunodeficiency virus.
questions.explanation: bloodborne pathogens: Pathogenic microorganisms that are present in human blood and can cause disease in humans. These pathogens include, but are not limited to, hepatitis B virus and human immunodeficiency virus.

questions.question: What does the term "posttraumatic stress disorder" mean?
choices: Reactions to stress that occur after a stressful situation.

A delayed stress reaction to a prior incident. Often the result of one or more unresolved issues concerning the incident, and may relate to an incident that involved physical harm or the threat of physical harm.
Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is caused by HIV, which damages the cells in the body's immune system so that the body is unable to fight infection or certain cancers.
The way in which an infectious disease is spread: contact, airborne, by vehicles, or by vectors.
questions.explanation: posttraumatic stress disorder: A delayed stress reaction to a prior incident. Often the result of one or more unresolved issues concerning the incident, and may relate to an incident that involved physical harm or the threat of physical harm.

questions.question: A crew member develops chickenpox days after transporting a shingles patient in a closed ambulance with poor ventilation. The virus most likely reached her by which route?
questions.explanation: Varicella virus can spread through the air via droplets and dust in an enclosed space.

questions.question: At a 2.5-hour choir practice in Mount Vernon, Washington in 2020, one symptomatic singer infected 53 of 61 attendees with COVID-19, and investigators concluded that aerosols from singing spread the virus through the shared indoor air. What should the EMT take from this case?
choices: Avoid entering any building where a group has gathered until the air has settled for a full day.
Assume respiratory viruses only spread by touch, so gloves alone are enough protection indoors.
Treat shared indoor air as a transmission route: mask up and ventilate on respiratory calls.
Focus only on disinfecting surfaces, since airborne spread cannot infect people across a room.
questions.explanation: Airborne transmission can move one infection through a whole room, so respiratory calls call for masking and ventilation.

questions.question: Navigate Case Study (EMT with delayed stress after a school bus MCI): What can you do to help yourself?
choices: Pick up extra shifts to stay busy, rely on caffeine to get through the day, and avoid counseling because it is only for severe cases.
Keep the experience to yourself so coworkers do not think you cannot handle the job, and wait for the feelings to pass on their own.

Recognize the warning signs of stress in yourself and act on them early. Talk with trusted coworkers, family, or a peer support team, and use professional help such as your agency's employee assistance program. Maintain a healthy lifestyle with regular exercise, proper diet, and adequate sleep, and use stress-management techniques such as relaxation and deep breathing.
Reduce your hours immediately and avoid any call involving children until you feel completely back to normal.
questions.explanation: Answer written from the chapter (no printed key).

questions.question: Which term is defined as: What type of sexual harassment occurs when the harasser requests sexual favors in exchange for something else, such as a promotion, a job benefit, a better shift, or a favorable evaluation.
questions.explanation: quid pro quo: What type of sexual harassment occurs when the harasser requests sexual favors in exchange for something else, such as a promotion, a job benefit, a better shift, or a favorable evaluation.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The body's response to stress that begins with an alarm response, followed by a stage of reaction and resistance, and then recovery or, if the stress is prolonged, exhaustion.
questions.explanation: general adaptation syndrome: The body's response to stress that begins with an alarm response, followed by a stage of reaction and resistance, and then recovery or, if the stress is prolonged, exhaustion.

questions.question: Assessment in Action: How can you help your partner to manage his stress?
choices: Suggest that he relax and have a few drinks after his shifts.
Suggest that the supervisor give him time off.

Suggest that he participate in physical activity away from the workplace. Emergency Care and Transportation of the Sick and Injured, Twelfth Edition AAOS Copyright © 2021 by Jones & Bartlett Learning, LLC an Ascend Learning Company. www.jblearning.com.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed answer key.

questions.question: During a Klebsiella pneumoniae outbreak in a hospital neonatal unit, investigators recovered the organism from the hands of 10% of the staff, and the official investigation attributed the spread in part to inadequate hand washing in an overcrowded nursery. What practice does this case demand of providers caring for high-risk patients such as infants?
choices: Restrict visitors to the unit, since staff hands are rarely the route of spread.
Wash hands thoroughly once at the start of the shift and after breaks.
Rely on gloves instead of hand washing when moving quickly between infants.
Wash hands between every patient, every time, especially with infants and other high-risk patients.
questions.explanation: The organism was recovered from staff hands, so hand washing between every patient is the control that stops the spread.

questions.question: What does the term "general adaptation syndrome" mean?
choices: The most effective way to preserve body heat when functioning in cold, wet weather — wearing at least three layers of clothing.

Protective measures that have traditionally been developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for use in dealing with objects, blood, body fluids, and other potential exposure risks of communicable disease; they are now officially referred to as standard precautions.
The body's response to stress that begins with an alarm response, followed by a stage of reaction and resistance, and then recovery or, if the stress is prolonged, exhaustion.
A beneficial response to a stressor.
questions.explanation: general adaptation syndrome: The body's response to stress that begins with an alarm response, followed by a stage of reaction and resistance, and then recovery or, if the stress is prolonged, exhaustion.

questions.question: What does the term "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention" mean?
choices: The primary federal agency that conducts and supports public health activities in the United States.
What type of sexual harassment occurs when the harasser requests sexual favors in exchange for something else, such as a promotion, a job benefit, a better shift, or a favorable evaluation.

The misuse of drugs or alcohol by a provider, on or off duty, that endangers the provider, coworkers, and patients; among EMS personnel, its most serious consequence is substandard or inappropriate patient care.
What airborne bacterial disease is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spreads when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and is indicated by a positive skin test showing exposure to the bacterium.
questions.explanation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: The primary federal agency that conducts and supports public health activities in the United States.
questions.topic: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

questions.question: Your service's exposure control plan requires a hepatitis B vaccination offer and sharps containers in every unit because of microorganisms that live in human blood. What hazard is the plan built around?
questions.explanation: The plan targets disease-causing microorganisms present in human blood, namely bloodborne pathogens such as HBV and HIV.

questions.question: After a week of short staffing and mandatory overtime, a paramedic reports headaches, poor sleep, and a feeling of being overwhelmed that is hurting his performance. What is this negative response to a stressor called?
questions.explanation: The stressor is producing a harmful, negative response in the provider, the definition of distress.

questions.question: A hemodialysis nurse got blood from a hepatitis C positive patient splashed into her face and eyes. She washed her eyes immediately and her first tests were negative, but about 6 months later she developed hepatitis C, confirmed by positive antibody and viral tests. What practice would have prevented this exposure?
choices: Skip follow-up testing once the first blood tests come back negative, since infection would already show.
Wear rated eye protection before the splash risk occurs, and treat every eye splash as a real exposure with flushing, reporting, and follow-up.
Rely on prescription glasses, which block most blood splashes from reaching the eyes.
Report the splash only if symptoms develop, to avoid unnecessary exposure paperwork.
questions.explanation: Blood can infect through the eyes alone, so rated eye protection is worn in advance and every splash gets flushing, reporting, and follow-up.

questions.question: Your exposure-control plan, your post-exposure follow-up steps, and the infection-control guidance your service follows all trace back to recommendations published by one federal agency. Which agency is it?
choices: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
questions.explanation: CDC is the primary federal public health agency and the source of the infection-control guidance EMS operates under.
questions.topic: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

questions.question: In late 1975, mothers in Lyme, Connecticut reported an unusual cluster of children with swollen joints diagnosed as juvenile arthritis. Yale researchers linked the illness to bites from deer ticks, and in 1982 the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi was identified inside the ticks. What should this case prompt an EMT to do when assessing outdoor and rural patients?
choices: Ask outdoor and rural patients about recent air travel and check their temperature before anything else.
Assume joint swelling in children is always a sports injury and skip questions about insect exposure.
Check only the patient's scalp for ticks, since ticks never attach anywhere else on the body.
Ask outdoor and rural patients about tick exposure and check for attached ticks and the bull's-eye rash during assessment.
questions.explanation: Lyme disease is spread by tick bites, so asking about tick exposure and checking for ticks and the bull's-eye rash catches it early.

questions.question: You transport a patient from a homeless shelter who has had a productive cough for 3 weeks, night sweats, weight loss, and coughing up blood. In the closed ambulance you wear a fit-tested N95 respirator and place a surgical mask on the patient. What disease should you suspect?
questions.explanation: Prolonged cough, night sweats, weight loss, and hemoptysis are classic signs, and it spreads airborne in enclosed spaces.

questions.question: A 26-year-old nurse was flushing the IV line of a patient in the terminal stages of AIDS when the patient jerked and the needle punctured her palm. Despite wound care, reporting, and postexposure prophylaxis, she was diagnosed with HIV about nine months later and later learned she also had hepatitis C. What is the sharps-safety lesson of this case?
choices: Hold the needle loosely so it drops harmlessly if the patient moves suddenly.
Treat every used sharp as loaded: control the patient, the needle, and your hands before you move.
Recap the needle as soon as the line is flushed so it cannot stick anyone.
Postexposure prophylaxis reliably prevents infection, so a stick is mainly a paperwork event.
questions.explanation: One moment with one used needle transmitted both HIV and hepatitis C; controlling the sharp before moving is the prevention.

questions.question: In 1999, six career firefighters died inside a six-story cold-storage warehouse fire in Worcester, Massachusetts, after becoming lost in near-zero visibility; four died from inhaling smoke, soot, and hot gases, and two from severe thermal injuries. What does this case require of EMTs at a working structure fire?
choices: Stage clear of the structure fire and let firefighters with SCBA and thermal imaging handle the interior search.
Ventilate the building by opening doors and windows to make interior conditions safer for entry.
Search the floors above the fire first, since smoke and heat are most dangerous at ground level.
Enter behind the first hose line without SCBA so treatment can start as soon as a victim is found.
questions.explanation: Heat, smoke, and toxic gases kill inside structure fires, so EMTs stage outside and leave interior search to firefighters in SCBA.

questions.question: In Dallas in 2014, two nurses were infected with Ebola while caring for a patient even though both had worn PPE, and the CDC responded by requiring no exposed skin and a trained monitor to watch donning and doffing. What is the practical lesson for EMS crews?
choices: Buddy-check your PPE before entry and after exit, because the doffing sequence is where exposures happen.
PPE failures mean the equipment is useless, so speed matters more than technique.
Only new employees need a PPE check; experienced providers can skip the buddy check.
Once PPE is on correctly, removing it in any order is safe.
questions.explanation: Standard precautions fail when PPE use is sloppy, so a trained observer should watch donning and doffing.

questions.question: While cleaning the ambulance, an EMT sticks her finger on a used IV needle left in the linen. The exposure concern is hepatitis B and HIV carried in the patient's blood. What group of microorganisms creates this risk?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B virus and HIV are pathogenic microorganisms present in human blood, which is the definition of bloodborne pathogens.

questions.question: Your department is writing its exposure control plan and must name the individual who will track crew exposures, arrange postexposure follow-up, and serve as liaison with medical facilities. What position must be named?
questions.explanation: Federal law and OSHA practice place exposure management and infection control responsibility on a named designated officer.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The tactical use of an impenetrable barrier for protection.
questions.explanation: cover: The tactical use of an impenetrable barrier for protection.

questions.question: What does the term "direct contact" mean?
choices: The body's response to stress that begins with an alarm response, followed by a stage of reaction and resistance, and then recovery or, if the stress is prolonged, exhaustion.
Exposure or transmission of a communicable disease from one person to another by physical contact.

The misuse of drugs or alcohol by a provider, on or off duty, that endangers the provider, coworkers, and patients; among EMS personnel, its most serious consequence is substandard or inappropriate patient care.
A combination of exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced performance resulting from long-term job stresses.
questions.explanation: direct contact: Exposure or transmission of a communicable disease from one person to another by physical contact.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: What PPE must be worn when blood or body fluids may splash into the eyes, noting that prescription glasses do not provide adequate protection because they offer little or no side protection.
questions.explanation: eye protection: What PPE must be worn when blood or body fluids may splash into the eyes, noting that prescription glasses do not provide adequate protection because they offer little or no side protection.

questions.question: An EMT who was energized by busy shifts last year now dreads the tones, has stomach aches before work, and snaps at her family after hard calls. The job's demands have become a harmful burden rather than a challenge. What type of stress response is she showing?
questions.explanation: Her response to the stressor is negative and damaging, which is distress rather than beneficial eustress.

questions.question: Navigate Case Study (EMT with delayed stress after a school bus MCI): How can poorly managed stress affect your job performance and overall career longevity?
choices: Poorly managed stress has little effect on job performance, because experienced EMTs can separate their feelings from patient care indefinitely.
Poorly managed stress affects only physical health; errors in patient care and early departure from EMS are caused by poor training instead.
Poorly managed stress improves job performance by keeping providers alert, and it has no relationship to how long an EMT stays in the profession.

Poorly managed stress impairs concentration and decision-making, which leads to errors in patient care and friction with patients and coworkers. Over time it produces cumulative stress reactions, burnout, and posttraumatic stress, drives absenteeism, and is a common reason EMTs leave the profession early.
questions.explanation: Answer written from the chapter (no printed key).

questions.question: A firefighter dies in a house fire. Forty-eight hours later, the firefighters who were on scene meet in a structured debriefing, led by trained CISM personnel, that is kept separate from any operational critique of the fire. What process is this?
questions.explanation: A line-of-duty death is a critical incident, and the formal 24-72 hour group session is the CISD.

questions.question: What does the term "communicable disease" mean?
choices: The abnormal invasion of a host or host tissues by organisms such as bacteria, viruses, or parasites, with or without signs or symptoms of disease.
A disease that can be spread from one person or species to another.
A combination of exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced performance resulting from long-term job stresses.

A sexually transmitted infectious disease caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum; unlike many infections, it confers no protection from reinfection after exposure, so a treated person can catch it again.
questions.explanation: communicable disease: A disease that can be spread from one person or species to another.

questions.question: What does the term "cover" mean?
choices: Pathogenic microorganisms that are present in human blood and can cause disease in humans. These pathogens include, but are not limited to, hepatitis B virus and human immunodeficiency virus.
The way in which an infectious disease is spread: contact, airborne, by vehicles, or by vectors.
A situation in which a person has had contact with blood, body fluids, tissues, or airborne particles and has the potential to develop a disease.
The tactical use of an impenetrable barrier for protection.
questions.explanation: cover: The tactical use of an impenetrable barrier for protection.

questions.question: After a call, an EMT realizes the patient's blood got into a cut on her hand. She fills out an exposure report and calls the one person in her department responsible for verifying the exposure and contacting the hospital for the source patient's test results. Who is she calling?
questions.explanation: Managing exposures and infection control follow-up for the department is the designated officer's assigned role.

questions.question: Teenager Ryan White was diagnosed with HIV in 1984 at age 13 after being infected through contaminated factor VIII blood product used to treat his hemophilia; he had no other risk factor. What does his case illustrate about bloodborne pathogens?
choices: Blood products carried risk only for hemophilia patients, not for anyone receiving a transfusion.
Hemophilia itself causes HIV infection, independent of any blood product the patient receives.
HIV spreads mainly through casual contact, which is why White's school barred him from attending.
A bloodborne pathogen can ride a blood product or any blood exposure, so no blood exposure should ever be treated as trivial.
questions.explanation: Blood is a vehicle for bloodborne pathogens; White's infection came entirely through a blood product.

questions.question: Unlike a reaction to one horrific scene, an EMT's burnout develops gradually over a year of relentless call volume and staffing shortages. Which type of stress reaction is this?
questions.explanation: It results from stress that is prolonged and excessive, accumulating call after call.

questions.question: A patient tells you he does not need testing because he 'already had syphilis and was cured last year, so he is immune now.' What is wrong with his reasoning?
questions.explanation: Syphilis confers no protection from reinfection after exposure; successful treatment does not make a person immune.

questions.question: A used lancet is found loose in the glove compartment, and the sharps container in the ambulance is stuffed past the fill line with needles poking out. What practice has broken down?
questions.explanation: Sharps must go immediately into a proper container, and overfilled containers cause exactly the sticks that transmit bloodborne viruses.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The way in which an infectious disease is spread: contact, airborne, by vehicles, or by vectors.
questions.explanation: transmission: The way in which an infectious disease is spread: contact, airborne, by vehicles, or by vectors.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Reactions to stress that occur after a stressful situation.
questions.explanation: delayed stress reactions: Reactions to stress that occur after a stressful situation.

questions.question: What does the term "standard precautions" mean?
choices: Pathogenic microorganisms that are present in human blood and can cause disease in humans. These pathogens include, but are not limited to, hepatitis B virus and human immunodeficiency virus.

Protective measures that have traditionally been developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for use in dealing with objects, blood, body fluids, and other potential exposure risks of communicable disease; they are now officially referred to as standard precautions.
Reactions to stress that occur after a stressful situation.
The body's response to stress that begins with an alarm response, followed by a stage of reaction and resistance, and then recovery or, if the stress is prolonged, exhaustion.
questions.explanation: standard precautions: Protective measures that have traditionally been developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for use in dealing with objects, blood, body fluids, and other potential exposure risks of communicable disease; they are now officially referred to as standard precautions.

questions.question: After an orca killed a trainer at SeaWorld Orlando in 2010, OSHA cited the park under the General Duty Clause of the OSH Act for exposing trainers to the recognized hazards of close contact with killer whales, even though no orca-specific standard existed; the citation was upheld in court in 2014. An employer in your district argues it has no duty to fix a recognized hazard because no specific OSHA standard covers it. Why is that wrong?
choices: It is not wrong; without a specific published standard, OSHA cannot cite any hazard.
The duty exists only if the hazard has already caused a fatality at that workplace.
Even without a specific standard, the employer still has a legal duty to protect employees from recognized dangers.
OSHA can act on an unlisted hazard only after employees petition Congress for a rule.
questions.explanation: Even without a specific standard for a hazard, your employer still has a legal duty to protect you from recognized dangers.

questions.question: A pharmacy's faucet and mixing container are found growing Serratia after patients get bloodstream infections from IV nutrition bags. What had happened to the product?
questions.explanation: The organisms were present in the product and its preparation equipment: contamination.

questions.question: Right after unloading a patient with C. difficile, you grab the ambulance door handle, then touch your face before washing your hands. Exposure through the contaminated handle is called what?
questions.explanation: The handle is a contaminated object (a fomite) between the patient and you.

questions.question: What does the term "designated officer" mean?
choices: The individual in the department who is charged with the responsibility of managing exposures and infection control.

What are the hazards at a structure fire that include possible building collapse, high heat, smoke and toxic gases, and oxygen-deficient air, and that require EMTs to stage at a safe distance and stay clear until the fire department declares the scene safe.
The capacity of an individual to cope with and recover from distress.
The most effective way to preserve body heat when functioning in cold, wet weather — wearing at least three layers of clothing.
questions.explanation: designated officer: The individual in the department who is charged with the responsibility of managing exposures and infection control.

questions.question: Your chief asks you to activate the regional team after a school bus rollover with multiple child fatalities, before stress reactions harden into bigger problems. Which program is she activating?
questions.explanation: CISM is the system designed to confront critical-incident responses early and defuse them.

questions.question: You are staged at a house fire. Firefighters report the roof is sagging, interior temperatures are extreme, and thick smoke is pushing from every opening. What hazard group is the main reason you must not enter to reach a patient?
questions.explanation: Collapse, high heat, and toxic smoke make the interior unsafe for EMTs without firefighter protection.

questions.question: In 2019, health officials alerted CDC to teenagers with severe lung injuries who had used vaping products; the national investigation that followed identified vitamin E acetate in illicit THC cartridges as the likely culprit after it was found in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients tested. You are assessing a young patient in severe respiratory distress with no signs of infection. What should you do?
choices: Ask only about cigarette smoking, since only tobacco smoke injures the lungs.
Ask specifically about vaping and THC cartridges; your history may be the clue that solves the case.
Document the cause as asthma and leave product use out of the patient care report.
Avoid asking about vaping, because e-cigarette use is not relevant to lung injury.
questions.explanation: Ask young respiratory-distress patients specifically about vaping and THC cartridges.
questions.topic: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

questions.question: After a needlestick from a used IV catheter, an EMT is sent for baseline testing for the virus that causes AIDS. Which virus is occupational health testing for?
questions.explanation: HIV is the virus that causes AIDS, and it is the bloodborne virus checked after a sharps exposure.

questions.question: Before suctioning a patient who is coughing up blood, you put on gloves, a mask, and eye protection. What is the collective name for the gear you just put on?
questions.explanation: Gloves, mask, and eye protection are equipment worn to block exposure to a pathogen, which is PPE.

questions.question: During a pediatric cardiac arrest call, your partner's hands shake, her heart pounds, and she feels frozen for a moment before she pushes through the call. These reactions happening during the event itself are called what?
questions.explanation: The shaking, pounding heart, and freeze response occurred during the stressful situation, which is what makes them acute.

questions.question: Researchers followed 12,822 World Trade Center responders for two decades and found that for many, PTSD symptoms peaked about 10 years after 9/11 rather than right after, with about 10% still showing elevated symptoms 20 years later. What does this pattern mean for looking after your partner?
choices: If a responder is fine at the one-month screening, no further follow-up is ever needed.
Only responders who showed symptoms immediately are at risk for long-term problems.
Check on partners months and years after bad calls, not just the week of the call.
Stress symptoms that appear years later are unrelated to the original incident and need no support.
questions.explanation: Stress reactions can peak a decade after the event, so follow-up has to continue for months and years.

questions.question: A New Zealand journal review of international evidence on compassion fatigue in paramedics found that its prevalence increases the longer a provider spends in the role. Job satisfaction, education, and regular monitoring of mental health were identified as key protectors. Based on this case, what should an EMS agency do?
choices: Because compassion fatigue rises with years spent in the role, the agency should use routine mental health check-ins, manageable workloads, and job satisfaction measures as frontline defenses.
The agency should rotate providers permanently out of patient care after five years.
Because it mainly affects new hires, the agency should focus support only during the first year.
Because compassion fatigue cannot be monitored, the agency should wait until a provider resigns.
questions.explanation: Compassion steadily lessens across a caregiving career, so ongoing monitoring and workload management are key defenses.

questions.question: Assessment in Action: Which of the following signs and symptoms are NOT usually associated with stress?
questions.explanation: From the book's printed answer key.

questions.question: You finish a call with a patient who has a draining MRSA wound, then immediately begin assessing the next patient without stopping at the sink or using sanitizer. Which basic infection-control step did you skip?
questions.explanation: Hand washing between patient contacts is the simplest, most effective way to stop carrying germs from one patient to the next.

questions.question: In fall 2014, Thomas Eric Duncan, who had traveled from Liberia, was treated for Ebola at a Dallas hospital. Two nurses who cared for him, Nina Pham and Amber Vinson, became infected, the first Ebola transmissions on US soil. What does this case teach about caring for a patient with a disease carried in body fluids?
choices: Assume any contact with the infected patient's body fluids during care is an exposure until proven otherwise.
Body fluids only become infectious after the patient's symptoms have peaked, so early care is low risk.
Routine gloves alone eliminate the risk, because hospital transmission of fluid-borne disease is not possible.
Exposure only counts if a sharps injury occurred, since intact skin contact with fluids is harmless.
questions.explanation: For a communicable disease carried in body fluids, any fluid contact during care is an exposure until proven otherwise.

questions.question: An EMT uses a blood pressure cuff on a patient with MRSA, then uses the same cuff on the next patient without disinfecting it, and that patient later develops MRSA. Transmission through the contaminated cuff is called what?
questions.explanation: The organism reached the second patient through a contaminated object, not by touching the first patient.

questions.question: An EMT had measles as a child. She cares for a measles patient without becoming ill, because her body already knows how to fight that virus. What is her body's protective ability called?
questions.explanation: Her body can protect itself from acquiring measles again, which is exactly what being immune means.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Cleaning and disinfecting the ambulance and its equipment after a call, including allowing disinfected surfaces to air dry unless otherwise indicated in the product directions, so the unit is safe for the next patient.
questions.explanation: ambulance decontamination: Cleaning and disinfecting the ambulance and its equipment after a call, including allowing disinfected surfaces to air dry unless otherwise indicated in the product directions, so the unit is safe for the next patient.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The spread of an organism via droplets or dust.
questions.explanation: airborne transmission: The spread of an organism via droplets or dust.

questions.question: What does the term "burnout" mean?
choices: Reactions to stress that occur during a stressful situation.

Securing a crashed vehicle with cribbing, struts, or other supports so it cannot move, shift, or roll; it must be done to ensure the vehicle is stable before attempting to access a patient trapped inside.
A combination of exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced performance resulting from long-term job stresses.
What PPE must be worn when blood or body fluids may splash into the eyes, noting that prescription glasses do not provide adequate protection because they offer little or no side protection.
questions.explanation: burnout: A combination of exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced performance resulting from long-term job stresses.

questions.question: An EMT develops a MRSA skin infection after her bare forearm, with broken skin from a scrape, pressed against a patient's infected wound during a lift. Which mode of transmission is this?
questions.explanation: The infection passed by physical skin-to-skin contact with infectious material — direct contact transmission.

questions.question: In 1907, New York cook Mary Mallon was identified as the first known healthy carrier of typhoid fever in the United States. Investigators linked her cooking to about 57 typhoid infections and 3 deaths, yet she never felt sick herself. What should an EMT take from this case when deciding on precautions?
choices: Skip respiratory precautions for patients with no fever, because a person without symptoms cannot spread disease.
Treat every patient as potentially infectious, because a carrier of a communicable disease may have no symptoms at all.
Rely on dispatch screening to flag infectious patients before arrival, since carriers are identified in advance.
Take full precautions only with patients who look or feel sick, since carriers usually show some symptoms.
questions.explanation: A carrier of a communicable disease may have no symptoms, so every patient is treated as potentially infectious.

questions.question: After a firefighter is hurt at a chemical plant, investigators from a federal agency arrive to check whether the employer followed workplace safety rules and can fine the company. Which agency is it?
choices: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health
questions.explanation: Investigating incidents and fining employers for safety violations is OSHA's enforcement role.

questions.question: In 1984, Indiana teenager Ryan White, who had hemophilia, was diagnosed with AIDS after receiving a contaminated factor VIII blood product. Doctors said he posed no casual-contact risk, yet he was barred from his middle school in 1985 and had to fight in court to attend. What does this case teach an EMT about caring for a patient with HIV?
choices: Patients with HIV should be transported only by crews who volunteer for infectious-disease calls.
HIV status never changes the care you give — use standard precautions and treat the patient with respect on every call.
HIV can spread through casual contact, so the crew should limit all physical contact with the patient.
A patient with HIV should be told to arrange private transport instead of using an ambulance.
questions.explanation: HIV spreads through blood, not casual contact, so standard precautions and respect are the correct response on every call.

questions.question: During the February 2021 Winter Storm Uri in Texas, 246 people died, and 158 of the deaths (64 percent) were from hypothermia. The state health department's report listed 'not wearing appropriate clothing or enough layering' among the risk factors for those deaths. What should an EMT take from this for cold-weather operations?
choices: Wear one heavy coat, which the report identified as equal to layered clothing for preventing heat loss.
