Dress in layers yourself and check patients and bystanders for inadequate clothing, not just injuries.
Assume people found indoors are safe from hypothermia and do not need a clothing check.
Focus only on treating injuries, since hypothermia deaths in disasters come from building failures, not clothing.
questions.explanation: Inadequate clothing and layering contributed to fatal heat loss, so EMTs layer up and check others' clothing during cold disasters.

questions.question: Your service is equipping crews for a forecasted blizzard shift with wet snow and subfreezing wind chills. The supply officer asks what minimum clothing setup each EMT should wear on calls. What do you tell her?
questions.explanation: Wearing at least three layers is the textbook's most effective way to preserve body heat in cold, wet conditions.

questions.question: While working a multi-casualty crash, you notice your own rapid breathing, tunnel vision, and racing heart as the scene unfolds around you. What are these in-the-moment responses called?
questions.explanation: They are stress reactions occurring while the stressful situation is still happening.

questions.question: Still on scene after a difficult call involving a child, an EMT feels numb, detached, and on edge. Reactions to stress that occur during a stressful situation are known as what?
questions.explanation: Feeling numb, detached, and on edge during the event are classic acute stress reactions.

questions.question: Your crew transports three residents from the same nursing home in one shift, all with vomiting and diarrhea traced to a norovirus multiplying in their digestive tracts. Each resident's condition is an example of what?
questions.explanation: A harmful organism spreading within each patient's body caused the illness, making each case an infectious disease.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The misuse of drugs or alcohol by a provider, on or off duty, that endangers the provider, coworkers, and patients; among EMS personnel, its most serious consequence is substandard or inappropriate patient care.
questions.explanation: substance abuse: The misuse of drugs or alcohol by a provider, on or off duty, that endangers the provider, coworkers, and patients; among EMS personnel, its most serious consequence is substandard or inappropriate patient care.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is caused by HIV, which damages the cells in the body's immune system so that the body is unable to fight infection or certain cancers.
questions.explanation: human immunodeficiency virus: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is caused by HIV, which damages the cells in the body's immune system so that the body is unable to fight infection or certain cancers.

questions.question: A clinic reuses a syringe to draw from a single-dose vial used for many patients, and hepatitis C spreads. The vial itself now carries the virus. What is that called?
questions.explanation: The vial holds infectious organisms on/in an object used on patients: contamination.

questions.question: The EEOC alleged that at a Las Vegas plumbing company, female employees who rejected sexual advances were threatened, while those who acquiesced were offered better work assignments and hours. The company agreed to pay $500,000 under a consent decree with training and an outside monitor. What rule does this case state for the workplace?
choices: Better assignments may be offered for sexual compliance as long as no one is demoted for refusing.
Only cash bonuses count as a job benefit, so shift and assignment offers cannot be quid pro quo.
Employees should settle such offers privately with the supervisor before involving management.
Better shifts or assignments must never be traded for sexual compliance; document and report any such offer.
questions.explanation: Trading better shifts or assignments for sexual compliance is quid pro quo harassment; document it and report it.

questions.question: Your patient has influenza and has been coughing in a small apartment where three family members also became sick this week. The illness passed from the patient to the family members in the home. What type of disease is this?
questions.explanation: It spread from one person to another, which is what makes a disease communicable.

questions.question: Two EMTs work the same difficult pediatric call. One feels focused and motivated afterward; the other feels shaky, tearful, and unable to concentrate for the rest of the shift. Which EMT is experiencing distress?
choices: an acute stress reaction (the first EMT)
questions.explanation: Distress is the negative response to a stressor; the same event can produce eustress in one person and distress in another.

questions.question: What does the term "airborne transmission" mean?
choices: The contamination of food or water with an organism that can cause disease.
What airborne bacterial disease is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spreads when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and is indicated by a positive skin test showing exposure to the bacterium.
The spread of an organism via droplets or dust.
The primary federal agency that conducts and supports public health activities in the United States.
questions.explanation: airborne transmission: The spread of an organism via droplets or dust.

questions.question: During the 2017 Route 91 Harvest festival shooting in Las Vegas, officers first took cover behind patrol vehicles under fire, then moved in pairs to a block wall for better protection. Why did they move?
choices: Patrol vehicles are better cover than walls, but the wall offered a clearer view of the crowd.
The wall put them closer to the shooter, which is the safest place to work from.
They moved because standing near vehicles is against policy during any shooting.
Only the masonry wall reliably stopped rounds, so they upgraded from vehicles to real cover as soon as they could.
questions.explanation: Responders move from concealment to real cover as soon as they can, and move patients with them.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (4-year-old girl in cardiac arrest): How can you psychologically prepare yourself for this call?
choices: Avoid thinking about the call on the way to the scene, and rely on your partner to handle anything you are not comfortable doing.
Take on as many difficult calls as possible early in your career so you become numb to stressful incidents quickly.
Mentally rehearse the worst possible outcome so that nothing you find on scene can surprise or affect you.

Know the job can be stressful and develop good coping mechanisms before and after an incident. Practice stress management regularly, know your own limitations, maintain a healthy lifestyle with proper sleep, healthy eating, and exercise, and do not take on more than you can handle.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A delayed stress reaction to a prior incident. Often the result of one or more unresolved issues concerning the incident, and may relate to an incident that involved physical harm or the threat of physical harm.
questions.explanation: posttraumatic stress disorder: A delayed stress reaction to a prior incident. Often the result of one or more unresolved issues concerning the incident, and may relate to an incident that involved physical harm or the threat of physical harm.

questions.question: A paramedic who treated victims of a mass shooting two years ago reports intrusive memories, emotional numbness, and trouble sleeping that have never fully gone away despite peer support. What condition should be suspected?
questions.explanation: Unresolved reactions tied to an earlier traumatic incident that involved harm and threat of harm point to PTSD.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A combination of exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced performance resulting from long-term job stresses.
questions.explanation: burnout: A combination of exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced performance resulting from long-term job stresses.

questions.question: You are posted outdoors for several hours at a winter MVC scene in rain and wind near freezing. Your partner wears one heavy coat over a cotton shirt and is soon soaked and shivering. What should you both have worn to preserve body heat?
questions.explanation: At least three layers trap heat and keep insulation working in cold, wet weather; one soaked coat does not.

questions.question: A veteran EMT notices growing irritability, loss of appetite, and trouble concentrating after months of overtime and difficult calls piling up. His chief recognizes the slow buildup as what?
questions.explanation: Prolonged or excessive stress accumulating over time produces cumulative stress reactions.

questions.question: A paramedic with 12 years on the job has felt drained for months. She has become cynical about patients, dreads every shift, and her assessments are not as sharp as they used to be after years of mandatory overtime. What has she developed?
questions.explanation: Exhaustion plus cynicism plus reduced performance building up from long-term job stress is the classic picture of burnout.

questions.question: Six months after completing penicillin treatment for syphilis, a man's follow-up blood test shows a fourfold rise in his RPR titer and he has a new painless sore. What most likely happened?
questions.explanation: A rising titer with new lesions after treatment signals a brand-new syphilis infection, because prior infection gives no immunity.

questions.question: A charge nurse reviewing survey results finds her long-serving EMS crews score lower on empathy measures every year they stay in the field. What phenomenon do the surveys describe?
questions.explanation: Compassion fatigue builds over time with years of caregiving, and studies show it rises with experience.

questions.question: Dispatch sends you to a school where a child with chickenpox has exposed an entire classroom. Your partner asks why the school nurse is sending exposure notices home to parents. What property of this illness makes the notices necessary?
questions.explanation: Chickenpox is communicable: it can be spread from one person to another, so every exposed classmate is at risk.

questions.question: Assessment in Action: On the basis of your partner’s actions, what is he most likely experiencing?
questions.explanation: From the book's printed answer key.

questions.question: Navigate Case Study (EMT with delayed stress after a school bus MCI): What are some of the factors that influence the reaction of a patient or family members to the stresses of an illness or injury?
choices: The nature and severity of the illness or injury, the level of pain, and fear of death or permanent disability all shape the reaction. Prior experiences with illness and health care, the patient's age, available family and social support, cultural and religious beliefs, financial concerns, and how clearly and compassionately providers communicate also play a role.
Reactions are determined by the diagnosis alone, so two patients with the same condition will always respond to the stress in the same way.
The reaction depends almost entirely on the patient's age; pain level, prior experiences, family support, and cultural beliefs have little influence.
The main factor is the cost of the ambulance transport; the severity of the illness and how providers communicate do not shape the reaction.
questions.explanation: Answer written from the chapter (no printed key).

questions.question: During an extrication, every push of the spreaders makes the car shift a little on its crushed suspension. What should the crew stop and correct before continuing?
questions.explanation: A vehicle that moves during tool work is not stabilized; the crew must secure it before patient access continues.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The individual in the department who is charged with the responsibility of managing exposures and infection control.
questions.explanation: designated officer: The individual in the department who is charged with the responsibility of managing exposures and infection control.

questions.question: What does the term "personal protective equipment" mean?
choices: A negative response to a stressor.
The body's response to stress that begins with an alarm response, followed by a stage of reaction and resistance, and then recovery or, if the stress is prolonged, exhaustion.

Securing a crashed vehicle with cribbing, struts, or other supports so it cannot move, shift, or roll; it must be done to ensure the vehicle is stable before attempting to access a patient trapped inside.
Protective equipment that blocks exposure to a pathogen or a hazardous material.
questions.explanation: personal protective equipment: Protective equipment that blocks exposure to a pathogen or a hazardous material.

questions.question: A firefighter felt fine after a fatal fire, but eight months later he has nightmares, avoids the station bay, and startles at tones. What type of stress reaction is this timing?
questions.explanation: The symptoms surfaced long after the event ended, which defines a delayed reaction.

questions.question: After a mass-casualty shooting, a defusing was held the same night. Your chief now schedules the longer, formal group debriefing for the responding EMTs and paramedics for the following evening, about 36 hours after the incident. What is that formal session?
questions.explanation: The defusing is the early, short session; the formal debriefing at 24-72 hours is the CISD.

questions.question: Two EMTs work the same fatal pediatric call. One uses peer support, sleeps, and is functioning normally within weeks; the other cannot shake the distress. The first EMT's ability to cope and bounce back is an example of what?
questions.explanation: Resilience is defined by coping with and recovering from distress rather than being overwhelmed by it.

questions.question: An outbreak of tuberculosis first detected in early 2024 in the Kansas City metro area grew to 68 confirmed active cases with 2 deaths before contact tracing and treatment brought it under control. Investigators found the disease had spread through prolonged shared air in the community. What does this mean for EMTs transporting a patient with a chronic cough from an affected area?
choices: Treat the call as low risk once the patient denies a formal TB diagnosis at the door.
Use airborne precautions for the patient and expect follow-up testing if a transport exposure is identified.
Use only standard precautions, because TB spreads mainly through contact with contaminated surfaces.
Avoid respirators during transport, since TB is only a risk inside hospital isolation rooms.
questions.explanation: TB spreads through prolonged shared air, so EMTs use airborne precautions and complete follow-up testing after an exposure.

questions.question: A patient with measles coughs in a small waiting room and leaves. An hour later another person enters, breathes the room air, and develops measles days later. This route of spread is called what?
questions.explanation: The measles virus stayed suspended in the air as fine droplets and dust after the patient left.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A disease that can be spread from one person or species to another.
questions.explanation: communicable disease: A disease that can be spread from one person or species to another.

questions.question: What does the term "ambulance decontamination" mean?
choices: The formal, structured group debriefing held 24 to 72 hours after a critical incident, as part of critical incident stress management (CISM), in which the responders involved discuss the incident and their reactions to it.
A situation in which a person has had contact with blood, body fluids, tissues, or airborne particles and has the potential to develop a disease.
The primary federal agency that conducts and supports public health activities in the United States.

Cleaning and disinfecting the ambulance and its equipment after a call, including allowing disinfected surfaces to air dry unless otherwise indicated in the product directions, so the unit is safe for the next patient.
questions.explanation: ambulance decontamination: Cleaning and disinfecting the ambulance and its equipment after a call, including allowing disinfected surfaces to air dry unless otherwise indicated in the product directions, so the unit is safe for the next patient.

questions.question: Over several months, a once-reliable EMT begins missing shifts, shows declining skills on calls, and is caught taking morphine from the drug safe. Coworkers agree the greatest danger from his behavior is not morale or discipline, but the care his patients receive. What is the underlying problem?
questions.explanation: Drug or alcohol abuse among EMS personnel is most serious because it leads to substandard or inappropriate patient care.

questions.question: What does the term "hand washing" mean?
choices: The simplest, yet most effective, method of preventing the spread of infectious disease: washing the hands in between patient contacts.
The federal regulatory compliance agency that develops, publishes, and enforces guidelines concerning employee safety.
What type of sexual harassment occurs when the harasser requests sexual favors in exchange for something else, such as a promotion, a job benefit, a better shift, or a favorable evaluation.

The misuse of drugs or alcohol by a provider, on or off duty, that endangers the provider, coworkers, and patients; among EMS personnel, its most serious consequence is substandard or inappropriate patient care.
questions.explanation: hand washing: The simplest, yet most effective, method of preventing the spread of infectious disease: washing the hands in between patient contacts.

questions.question: You transport a patient from a homeless encampment who has yellowed eyes, nausea, and no appetite. The hospital later confirms a viral infection that inflames the liver and is spreading through the encampment. What condition does this patient have?
questions.explanation: Jaundice, nausea, and appetite loss are the classic signs of an inflamed, virus-infected liver.

questions.question: Between patients, a crew wipes down the stretcher, changes gloves, washes hands, and bags contaminated trash before the next call. Together, these steps are known as what?
questions.explanation: These are procedures done specifically to reduce transmission of infection among patients and health care personnel.

questions.question: A paramedic is told by the chief who approves promotions that she will not be promoted unless she has sex with him. She refuses and is passed over. What type of sexual harassment occurred?
questions.explanation: Promotion was conditioned on sex, and refusal brought a job loss.

questions.question: What does the term "infectious disease" mean?
choices: Inflammation of the liver, usually caused by a viral infection, that causes fever, loss of appetite, nausea, intestinal upset, and often jaundice.
The body's ability to protect itself from acquiring a disease.
A medical condition caused by the growth and spread of small, harmful organisms within the body.
Exposure or transmission of a communicable disease from one person to another by physical contact.
questions.explanation: infectious disease: A medical condition caused by the growth and spread of small, harmful organisms within the body.

questions.question: In 1936, Hans Selye exposed rats to completely different stressors — cold, surgical injury, excessive exercise, and sub-lethal drug doses — and all showed the same staged response: an alarm reaction, then resistance, then exhaustion if the stress continued. What is the lesson for responders?
choices: The body answers every major stressor with the same staged pattern, so manage your total stress load, not just one call at a time.
Only physical stressors like injury trigger the body's staged stress response.
Each type of stressor produces a completely separate response, so stresses never add together.
Once the resistance stage is reached, the body can handle unlimited stress without exhaustion.
questions.explanation: Your body answers every major stressor with the same staged pattern, so manage total stress load, not just one call at a time.

questions.question: Your crew regularly responds to a homeless encampment where hepatitis A is spreading person-to-person; the San Diego outbreak of this kind grew to more than 580 cases with 20 deaths, and the county response relied on mass vaccination, handwashing stations, and street sanitation. What should EMTs serving these patients treat as frontline hepatitis prevention?
choices: Treat vaccination and hand hygiene as frontline hepatitis prevention when serving homeless patients.
Give antibiotics to every patient from the encampment as a precaution against the virus.
Avoid transporting any patient from the encampment until the outbreak is declared over.
Rely on gloves alone and skip handwashing once the gloves come off.
questions.explanation: Vaccination and hand hygiene are frontline hepatitis prevention when serving homeless patients.

questions.question: Your crew transports a patient who tells you he has been HIV-positive for years. A trainee asks why HIV is so serious if it is 'just a virus.' The danger is that this virus destroys the cells of which body system?
choices: hepatitis C virus — it destroys the liver's filtering cells
human immunodeficiency virus — it destroys the nerve cells that control breathing
human immunodeficiency virus — it destroys the red blood cells that carry oxygen
human immunodeficiency virus — it destroys the immune system's cells
questions.explanation: HIV attacks the immune cells themselves, leaving the body unable to fight infections and some cancers.

questions.question: Navigate Case Study (EMT with delayed stress after a school bus MCI): What are other proven methods for decreasing the adverse effects of stress overall?
choices: Keeping feelings private, skipping meals during busy shifts, and relying on energy drinks to stay alert are proven ways to reduce the effects of stress.
Working longer shifts to build tolerance, using tobacco or alcohol in moderation to relax, and avoiding exercise on days off so the body can fully rest.

Regular physical exercise, a healthy diet, and adequate sleep are the foundation. Relaxation techniques such as meditation and deep breathing, strong social support from family and coworkers, critical incident stress management, and professional counseling through an employee assistance program are also proven, while limiting alcohol, caffeine, and tobacco helps.
Stress cannot be reduced once symptoms appear; the only proven approach is to leave EMS work entirely before symptoms develop.
questions.explanation: Answer written from the chapter (no printed key).

questions.question: In July 1998, nurse Karen Daley was stuck by a needle protruding from an overfilled sharps container at Brigham and Women's Hospital. That single needlestick infected her with both HIV and hepatitis C, and her advocacy led to the federal Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act. What sharps practice does her case demand of EMTs?
choices: Recap used needles before disposal to conserve space in the sharps container.
Fill sharps containers above the line during busy shifts and empty them at the end of the week.
Carry a used needle to the container by hand if the container is more than a few steps away.
Never overfill a sharps container and never carry a used needle loose; dispose of sharps properly every time.
questions.explanation: One used needle carried two bloodborne pathogens; never overfill a sharps container or carry a used needle loose.

questions.question: Your crew stages behind a large dumpster across the street from a reported shooting so the suspect cannot see the ambulance. What is this tactic called?
questions.explanation: The dumpster blocks the shooter's view but would not stop a bullet, so it hides you rather than protecting you.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The most effective way to preserve body heat when functioning in cold, wet weather — wearing at least three layers of clothing.
questions.explanation: cold-weather clothing layers: The most effective way to preserve body heat when functioning in cold, wet weather — wearing at least three layers of clothing.

questions.question: Assessment in Action: Which of the following is NOT a recommended way to manage stress?
questions.explanation: From the book's printed answer key.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (4-year-old girl in cardiac arrest): How can you mitigate the stress associated with the job?
choices: Avoid thinking or talking about stressful calls altogether, since discussing them only makes the stress worse over time.
Keep work stress separate by avoiding coworkers off duty, skip debriefings, and use alcohol in moderation to unwind after difficult calls.

Maintain a healthy lifestyle, including regular exercise, a healthy diet, and adequate sleep. Use stress-management techniques such as relaxation, meditation, and deep breathing, seek social support from family, friends, and coworkers, recognize the warning signs of stress, and seek professional help if needed.
Take on extra overtime shifts so that stressful calls become routine, and rely on caffeine to stay alert through long shifts.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.

questions.question: A paramedic who smokes decides to quit, joins a cessation program, and tracks his blood pressure monthly with the department nurse. Which idea best describes what he is doing?
questions.explanation: Quitting smoking and monitoring his health are deliberate actions in pursuit of good health, which is wellness.

questions.question: In the 1998-99 Nipah outbreak in Malaysia, Pteropus fruit bats were the natural reservoir hosts of the virus, and domestic pigs became amplifying hosts that caught it from bats and passed it to farm workers, causing 265 human cases. What does this host chain mean for patient assessment?
choices: The outbreak spread only from person to person, so animal hosts played no real role in transmission.
Ask about animal exposures during assessment, because the host chain behind a patient's illness often runs through animals first.
Animal contact is irrelevant to a human infection history once the patient shows symptoms.
The pigs were the original natural reservoir, so only pig exposure needs to be asked about.
questions.explanation: Nipah reached humans through two kinds of host, so animal exposure history matters on assessment.

questions.question: What does the term "concealment" mean?
choices: A medical condition caused by the growth and spread of small, harmful organisms within the body.
The use of objects to limit a person's ability to see you.
The organism or individual that is attacked by the infecting agent.
A negative response to a stressor.
questions.explanation: concealment: The use of objects to limit a person's ability to see you.

questions.question: Two bombs exploded near the Boston Marathon finish line on April 15, 2013, killing 3 spectators and wounding more than 260 people. Medical tent volunteers and responders treated severe blast injuries, including many amputations. Ten years later, responders still described intrusive thoughts, nightmares, and anxiety, and a hospital support group was treating classic PTSD symptoms. What is the main lesson of this case?
choices: Only responders who were physically injured at the scene are at risk for lasting PTSD.
Symptoms lasting more than a year mean the responder was unfit for duty from the start.
PTSD after a mass-casualty event resolves on its own once the responder returns to a normal schedule.
Even after a well-run, successful response, PTSD symptoms can persist for years, so planned long-term follow-up matters as much as the initial debriefing.
questions.explanation: PTSD is a delayed, persistent reaction that can follow even a single well-handled incident.

questions.question: After the September 11, 2001 attacks, FDNY firefighters and EMS responders worked rescue and recovery at Ground Zero. Federal monitoring later found nearly 20% of responders were diagnosed with World Trade Center-related PTSD, and about half of the mental health disorders did not appear until 11 to 13 years after the exposure. What does this case illustrate about PTSD in responders?
choices: PTSD only develops in responders who showed obvious symptoms at the scene.
A single critical incident debriefing held right after the event is enough to prevent PTSD.
Responders who stay busy and avoid talking about the event rarely develop PTSD.
PTSD can be a delayed reaction that surfaces years after the incident, so responders need monitoring and follow-up long after the event, not just in the weeks after it.
questions.explanation: PTSD is a delayed stress reaction; symptoms may emerge years after the traumatic incident.

questions.question: What does the term "transmission" mean?
choices: The way in which an infectious disease is spread: contact, airborne, by vehicles, or by vectors.
The primary federal agency that conducts and supports public health activities in the United States.

Protective measures that have traditionally been developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for use in dealing with objects, blood, body fluids, and other potential exposure risks of communicable disease; they are now officially referred to as standard precautions.
The contamination of food or water with an organism that can cause disease.
questions.explanation: transmission: The way in which an infectious disease is spread: contact, airborne, by vehicles, or by vectors.

questions.question: Ohio State researchers gave identical small punch-biopsy wounds to 13 women caring for relatives with dementia and 13 matched controls. The caregivers' wounds took about 24% longer to heal (48.7 versus 39.3 days). What does this demonstrate?
choices: Stress affects only mood and has no measurable effect on immune function or healing.
Caregivers' slower healing was caused by the wound care products they used at home.
Chronic stress measurably weakens the immune system and healing, making long-term overload a physical injury risk, not just a mood problem.
Wound healing speed is fixed by age and genetics and cannot be changed by stress.
questions.explanation: Chronic stress measurably weakens your immune system and healing; long-term overload is a physical injury risk, not just a mood problem.

questions.question: A city issues a boil-water order after E. coli is found in the municipal supply, and your station begins running calls for dehydrated elderly patients with gastroenteritis. What transmission route is involved?
questions.explanation: The definition covers contamination of food or water with a disease-causing organism.

questions.question: What does the term "human immunodeficiency virus" mean?
choices: A beneficial response to a stressor.
Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is caused by HIV, which damages the cells in the body's immune system so that the body is unable to fight infection or certain cancers.
Reactions to stress that occur during a stressful situation.
Handling needles and other sharps carefully and disposing of them properly; careless handling of sharps is the usual route by which HIV and hepatitis are spread in health care settings.
questions.explanation: human immunodeficiency virus: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is caused by HIV, which damages the cells in the body's immune system so that the body is unable to fight infection or certain cancers.

questions.question: On September 28, 2014, a Dallas Fire-Rescue crew transported Thomas Eric Duncan, who became the first Ebola case diagnosed in the United States. The three crew members were placed in home isolation for 21 days, and the ambulance stayed in service for about 48 hours before it was quarantined, exposing gaps in notification. What does this case teach about infection control before the patient is ever loaded?
choices: Infection control begins only after arrival at the hospital, when the receiving facility takes over screening.
Crews should refuse transport for any patient with a fever until a physician clears them by phone.
Travel history and dispatch screening are infection control: identify the risk before the patient is in your ambulance.
The ambulance should be returned to service immediately after any transport to keep the fleet available.
questions.explanation: The Dallas Ebola transport showed that travel history and dispatch screening identify the risk before the patient is in the ambulance.

questions.question: Two firefighters are exposed to the same patient with chickenpox. The one who had the varicella vaccine stays healthy; the one with no prior exposure or vaccine gets sick. What did the vaccine give the first firefighter?
questions.explanation: The vaccine made his body able to protect itself from acquiring the disease, while his partner had no such protection.

questions.question: Your crew wants to clear the hospital quickly, so the back of the ambulance gets no cleaning after a call involving a patient with diarrhea and a fever. What required task is being skipped?
questions.explanation: The patient compartment must be cleaned and disinfected after every call, or the next patient rides in the last patient's germs.

questions.question: After months of back-to-back overdose and cardiac arrest calls, a paramedic tells his partner, 'I used to care about these people. Now I just go through the motions.' What stress disorder is developing?
questions.explanation: Caring capacity erodes gradually with cumulative exposure, which is compassion fatigue rather than a single-incident reaction.

questions.question: What does the term "eye protection" mean?
choices: What PPE must be worn when blood or body fluids may splash into the eyes, noting that prescription glasses do not provide adequate protection because they offer little or no side protection.
Exposure or transmission of a communicable disease from one person to another by physical contact.
What type of sexual harassment occurs when the harasser requests sexual favors in exchange for something else, such as a promotion, a job benefit, a better shift, or a favorable evaluation.
Reactions to stress that occur after a stressful situation.
questions.explanation: eye protection: What PPE must be worn when blood or body fluids may splash into the eyes, noting that prescription glasses do not provide adequate protection because they offer little or no side protection.

questions.question: After the September 11, 2001 attacks, FDNY screened 8,487 firefighters; 76% reported at least one PTSD symptom, about 12% met criteria for elevated PTSD risk, and a follow-up study found nearly half of probable PTSD cases were delayed onset, appearing 3–4 years later. What should responders and their departments take from this?
choices: Responders should wait until symptoms interfere with work before seeking any help.
Screening after a major incident is unnecessary if crews seem fine in the first few weeks.
Symptoms that appear years later are unrelated to the original incident and need no support.
Delayed symptoms are normal — use peer support and counseling early, before stress compounds.
questions.explanation: Months of recovery work on top of losing 343 coworkers produced stress reactions that kept emerging for years.

questions.question: What does the term "delayed stress reactions" mean?
choices: The abnormal invasion of a host or host tissues by organisms such as bacteria, viruses, or parasites, with or without signs or symptoms of disease.
The federal regulatory compliance agency that develops, publishes, and enforces guidelines concerning employee safety.
Reactions to stress that occur after a stressful situation.

Protective measures that have traditionally been developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for use in dealing with objects, blood, body fluids, and other potential exposure risks of communicable disease; they are now officially referred to as standard precautions.
questions.explanation: delayed stress reactions: Reactions to stress that occur after a stressful situation.

questions.question: Researchers studied 181 firefighters who worked rescue and recovery after the Oklahoma City bombing and found only 13% developed bombing-related PTSD, significantly less than the 23% rate in male direct survivors; the authors credited career selection, training, preparedness, experience, and post-disaster mental health interventions. What does this case illustrate?
choices: Seeking counseling after a disaster is what causes responders' symptoms to increase.
Only responders who show no symptoms at all after a disaster are truly recovering.
Training, experience, and crew support measurably raise a responder's capacity to recover from a horrific call.
Responders recover best when they avoid any discussion of the event afterward.
questions.explanation: Training, experience, and crew support measurably raise a responder's capacity to recover from a horrific call.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The use of an animal to spread an organism from one person or place to another.
questions.explanation: vector-borne transmission: The use of an animal to spread an organism from one person or place to another.

questions.question: What does the term "acute stress reactions" mean?
choices: Reactions to stress that occur after a stressful situation.

Securing a crashed vehicle with cribbing, struts, or other supports so it cannot move, shift, or roll; it must be done to ensure the vehicle is stable before attempting to access a patient trapped inside.
Reactions to stress that occur during a stressful situation.
The tactical use of an impenetrable barrier for protection.
questions.explanation: acute stress reactions: Reactions to stress that occur during a stressful situation.

questions.question: What does the term "structural fire hazards" mean?
choices: Any airway manipulation that induces the production of aerosols that may present a risk for airborne transmission of pathogens, such as during CPR.

Protective measures that have traditionally been developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for use in dealing with objects, blood, body fluids, and other potential exposure risks of communicable disease; they are now officially referred to as standard precautions.

What are the hazards at a structure fire that include possible building collapse, high heat, smoke and toxic gases, and oxygen-deficient air, and that require EMTs to stage at a safe distance and stay clear until the fire department declares the scene safe.
The individual in the department who is charged with the responsibility of managing exposures and infection control.
questions.explanation: structural fire hazards: What are the hazards at a structure fire that include possible building collapse, high heat, smoke and toxic gases, and oxygen-deficient air, and that require EMTs to stage at a safe distance and stay clear until the fire department declares the scene safe.

questions.question: NFPA counted 62 on-duty firefighter deaths in the United States in 2024. Overexertion and strain caused 40 of them, and 30 of those were heart attacks; US Fire Administration guidance notes sudden cardiac events account for nearly 45% of firefighter line-of-duty deaths in recent years. What is the main lesson of these statistics?
choices: On-duty deaths are mainly caused by trauma, so health screening is a low priority.
Because sudden cardiac events are the leading killer of firefighters, fitness, sleep, and medical screening are life-safety equipment, and wellness is a safety program.
Wellness only matters for older firefighters nearing retirement.
Cardiac deaths are unavoidable in the fire service, so screening has little value.
questions.explanation: The leading killer of firefighters is a health condition, which is why wellness, the active pursuit of good health, is a safety program.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Inflammation of the liver, usually caused by a viral infection, that causes fever, loss of appetite, nausea, intestinal upset, and often jaundice.
questions.explanation: hepatitis: Inflammation of the liver, usually caused by a viral infection, that causes fever, loss of appetite, nausea, intestinal upset, and often jaundice.

questions.question: At a scene with a spilled chemical, the hazmat officer stops you and says your turnout gear alone is not enough; you need the issued chemical suit and gloves before entry. What is he requiring you to wear?
questions.explanation: The suit and gloves are protective equipment that blocks exposure to a hazardous material, which is PPE.

questions.question: What does the term "wellness" mean?
choices: Exposure or transmission of a communicable disease from one person to another by physical contact.
The active pursuit of a state of good health.
The spread of an organism via droplets or dust.
What PPE must be worn when blood or body fluids may splash into the eyes, noting that prescription glasses do not provide adequate protection because they offer little or no side protection.
questions.explanation: wellness: The active pursuit of a state of good health.

questions.question: Two wrestlers share a mat, and one gives the other a herpes skin infection through skin-to-skin contact during a match. EMS documents the transmission route as what?
questions.explanation: The virus moved from person to person by physical contact, the definition of direct contact.

questions.question: First responders screened after Hurricane Katrina were checked again 13 to 18 months after the storm, and their PTSD and depression symptoms had not significantly decreased by the second screening. What should an agency build into its disaster response based on this?
choices: Assume persistent symptoms a year later mean the responder was unfit for the work all along.
End all peer support at demobilization, since symptoms resolve on their own within weeks.
Screen responders only once, immediately after the deployment ends.
Build peer-support check-ins into the year after a disaster deployment, not just the demobilization week.
questions.explanation: Reactions can stay active well over a year after a response ends, so support must extend into the following year.

questions.question: A strange cluster of lung injuries in healthy young patients is reported by several states, and a federal agency coordinates the national investigation, lab testing, and public alerts. Which agency leads that work?
choices: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
questions.explanation: Coordinating multistate outbreak investigations is CDC's core public health role.
questions.topic: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

questions.question: At Hong Kong's Prince of Wales Hospital in 2003, 138 people were infected with SARS within two weeks in a ward where the index patient received jet-nebulized salbutamol treatments on an open ward. When protocols allow for an infectious respiratory patient, what should the EMT prefer?
choices: Prefer a metered-dose inhaler over a nebulizer for infectious respiratory patients when protocols allow.
Run the nebulizer continuously during transport to keep the medication flowing.
Nebulizers are safer than inhalers because the mist traps the virus before it spreads.
Remove the patient's mask during nebulizer treatments so the aerosols can escape freely.
questions.explanation: The nebulizer turned one patient's virus into room-wide aerosols, so inhalers are preferred when protocols allow.

questions.question: A department builds sleep, exercise, and peer-support habits into the schedule specifically so medics can recover from distress and keep doing the job for years. What are they trying to build?
questions.explanation: Those habits are aimed at the capacity to cope with and recover from distress — resilience.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Procedures to reduce transmission of infection among patients and health care personnel.
questions.explanation: infection control: Procedures to reduce transmission of infection among patients and health care personnel.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Any airway manipulation that induces the production of aerosols that may present a risk for airborne transmission of pathogens, such as during CPR.
questions.explanation: aerosol-generating procedure: Any airway manipulation that induces the production of aerosols that may present a risk for airborne transmission of pathogens, such as during CPR.

questions.question: What does the term "distress" mean?
choices: The spread of an organism via droplets or dust.
A negative response to a stressor.
The use of objects to limit a person's ability to see you.
The individual in the department who is charged with the responsibility of managing exposures and infection control.
questions.explanation: distress: A negative response to a stressor.

questions.question: You find a used IV catheter left uncapped on the squad bench and lab later grows bacteria from a vial it touched. What term describes organisms present on that equipment?
questions.explanation: Infectious organisms sitting on an object is contamination of that object.

questions.question: After a call, your partner asks what made the patient sick. You explain that a microscopic organism capable of causing disease in a susceptible host was responsible. That organism is called what?
questions.explanation: A pathogen is by definition a microorganism that can cause disease in a susceptible host.

questions.question: In August 1999, an outbreak of encephalitis struck Queens, New York City, at the same time as a large die-off of crows and exotic birds at the Bronx Zoo. Investigators identified West Nile virus, never before recorded in the Western Hemisphere; 62 human cases were confirmed and 7 people died. The virus was carried from infected birds to humans by Culex pipiens mosquitoes. What should EMS crews take from this case?
choices: Crews should assume encephalitis clusters are spread person to person and wear respirators on every outdoor call.
Crews should focus on the sick birds as the direct source and handle dead birds without gloves to speed up the scene.
Crews should avoid outdoor scenes entirely during mosquito season until public health clears the area.
Crews should treat clusters of encephalitis in mosquito season as a possible arbovirus event and use repellent and skin coverage on outdoor scenes.
questions.explanation: Mosquitoes acting as vectors carried West Nile virus from birds to people, so repellent and skin coverage protect crews during mosquito season.

questions.question: A man in Miami develops Zika after local mosquitoes bite him; he never traveled. What term describes the mosquito route that infected him?
questions.explanation: A living carrier such as a mosquito is a vector, and spread by vectors is transmission.

questions.question: Thomas Eric Duncan arrived in Dallas from Liberia in September 2014 and became the first Ebola case diagnosed in the United States; he died on October 8, 2014. His recent travel from an outbreak region was a key fact in recognizing the danger. What practice does this case highlight for EMS crews?
choices: Patients arriving from overseas should be refused transport until public health clears them.
Travel history matters only for patients who already have a confirmed diagnosis.
Ask where a febrile patient has traveled — travel history is a vital sign.
Ask about travel only after the patient reaches the hospital, to avoid delaying transport.
questions.explanation: A single imported case can bring an overseas pathogen into a US emergency department without warning, so travel history must be asked early.

questions.question: What does the term "resilience" mean?
choices: The federal regulatory compliance agency that develops, publishes, and enforces guidelines concerning employee safety.
The capacity of an individual to cope with and recover from distress.
Protective equipment that blocks exposure to a pathogen or a hazardous material.

A delayed stress reaction to a prior incident. Often the result of one or more unresolved issues concerning the incident, and may relate to an incident that involved physical harm or the threat of physical harm.
questions.explanation: resilience: The capacity of an individual to cope with and recover from distress.

questions.question: After a possible measles exposure on a call, your medical director checks the national case counts and the latest vaccine recommendations before updating your protocol. Which federal agency publishes both?
choices: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
questions.explanation: CDC conducts national disease surveillance and issues the vaccine recommendations used in U.S. public health.
questions.topic: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

questions.question: After a summer of heavy rain, mosquitoes multiply around a Florida neighborhood. Several residents with no travel history develop dengue fever, and trapped mosquitoes test positive for the virus. What type of transmission is responsible?
questions.explanation: The mosquitoes are the living carriers moving the virus from person to person, so the spread is vector-borne.

questions.question: Eight months after working a fatal apartment fire where two children died, an EMT still has nightmares about the scene, avoids driving past the building, and startles badly at the sound of a smoke alarm. What stress disorder best fits this picture?
questions.explanation: The symptoms are a delayed reaction to a prior incident, appearing and persisting long after the event itself.

questions.question: After starting an IV, an EMT drops the used needle onto the stretcher instead of into the sharps container, and his partner is stuck when she reaches for a blanket. Which safety failure caused this exposure?
questions.explanation: Careless handling of sharps is the usual way HIV and hepatitis spread to health care workers.

questions.question: A new EMT asks which single habit prevents more infections than any glove, mask, or gown. What is the answer?
choices: disinfecting the ambulance after each call
questions.explanation: Clean hands between contacts break the chain of transmission more reliably than any single piece of equipment.

questions.question: Assessment in Action: What are the long-term psychological effects of stress?
choices: Long-term psychological reactions to stress include fear, dull or nonresponsive behavior, depression, guilt, oversensitivity, anger, irritability, and frustration.
Long-term psychological reactions to stress include euphoria, increased confidence, sharpened focus, and a lasting sense of calm.
Long-term psychological reactions to stress include hallucinations, delusions, and a complete loss of contact with reality.
Long-term psychological reactions to stress are limited to brief sadness that resolves on its own within one shift.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed answer key.

questions.question: Through February 2020, Kirkland, Washington firefighters answered about 30 medical calls at a nursing home where COVID-19 was spreading, up from 7 calls the month before, without knowing the virus was inside. On February 29 the city quarantined 25 firefighters and 2 police officers, and roughly a third of the department ended up in quarantine or isolation. What is the key staffing lesson?
choices: One unprotected transport can sideline a whole crew — PPE protects staffing as well as health.
Crews should keep answering calls at an outbreak facility without PPE to maintain staffing.
Exposure tracking only matters once a responder tests positive.
Quarantine after repeated facility calls is an overreaction if no responder feels sick.
questions.explanation: Repeated routine calls created repeated exposures before anyone knew the pathogen was there, sidelining much of the department.

questions.question: What does the term "tuberculosis" mean?
choices: The misuse of drugs or alcohol by a provider, on or off duty, that endangers the provider, coworkers, and patients; among EMS personnel, its most serious consequence is substandard or inappropriate patient care.
A beneficial response to a stressor.
What airborne bacterial disease is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spreads when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and is indicated by a positive skin test showing exposure to the bacterium.
The simplest, yet most effective, method of preventing the spread of infectious disease: washing the hands in between patient contacts.
questions.explanation: tuberculosis: What airborne bacterial disease is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spreads when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and is indicated by a positive skin test showing exposure to the bacterium.

questions.question: A national study of U.S. paramedics found more than 20 percent are exposed to blood each year. Half of mucous membrane exposures were caused by the patient vomiting, spitting, or coughing up blood, a third involved an uncooperative or combative patient, and a third happened even though the paramedic was wearing eye or face protection. What is the right response to these findings?
choices: Rely on a surgical mask alone, because most splashes strike the mouth rather than the eyes.
Skip eye protection with combative patients, since it is likely to be knocked off anyway.
Put on well-fitting rated eye protection before patient contact, because EMS eye exposures are sudden and patient-driven.
Put eye protection on only after a patient starts vomiting or bleeding, when the risk becomes clear.
questions.explanation: Eye exposures in EMS are sudden and patient-driven, so rated, well-fitting eye protection goes on before patient contact.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Protective measures that have traditionally been developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for use in dealing with objects, blood, body fluids, and other potential exposure risks of communicable disease; they are now officially referred to as standard precautions.
questions.explanation: standard precautions: Protective measures that have traditionally been developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for use in dealing with objects, blood, body fluids, and other potential exposure risks of communicable disease; they are now officially referred to as standard precautions.

questions.question: Mary Mallon, a New York cook identified in 1907, carried typhoid bacteria in nearly every stool sample and was linked to about 51 infections, yet she felt completely healthy the entire time. What does her case show?
choices: Carriers only spread disease during the days when they feel sick themselves.
Lab tests that find organisms in a healthy-feeling person are almost always false positives.
A person who looks and feels healthy can still carry an infection and spread it to others.
A person with no signs or symptoms cannot be carrying any transmissible organism.
questions.explanation: A patient or food handler who looks and feels healthy can still carry and spread an infection.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Exposure or transmission of a communicable disease from one person to another by physical contact.
questions.explanation: direct contact: Exposure or transmission of a communicable disease from one person to another by physical contact.

questions.question: In 1976, about 182 American Legion convention attendees at a Philadelphia hotel developed pneumonia and 29 died. Investigators traced the new bacterium, Legionella pneumophila, to the hotel cooling tower, spread through the air-conditioning system with no person-to-person spread. What does this case illustrate?
choices: An outbreak with no person-to-person spread must have been caused by contaminated food or water.
Airborne spread can come from building systems, not just patients, so the air in enclosed spaces must be treated as a possible route.
Bacteria in a building's air system are harmless because ventilation always dilutes them to safe levels.
Airborne organisms can only be spread when a sick person coughs directly onto another person.
questions.explanation: Airborne spread can come from building systems, not just patients, so treat the air in enclosed spaces as a possible route.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The formal, structured group debriefing held 24 to 72 hours after a critical incident, as part of critical incident stress management (CISM), in which the responders involved discuss the incident and their reactions to it.
questions.explanation: critical incident stress debriefing: The formal, structured group debriefing held 24 to 72 hours after a critical incident, as part of critical incident stress management (CISM), in which the responders involved discuss the incident and their reactions to it.

questions.question: What does the term "hepatitis" mean?
choices: Inflammation of the liver, usually caused by a viral infection, that causes fever, loss of appetite, nausea, intestinal upset, and often jaundice.
The individual in the department who is charged with the responsibility of managing exposures and infection control.
A stress disorder characterized by gradual lessening of compassion over time.
The presence of infectious organisms on or in objects such as dressings, water, food, needles, wounds, or a patient's body.
questions.explanation: hepatitis: Inflammation of the liver, usually caused by a viral infection, that causes fever, loss of appetite, nausea, intestinal upset, and often jaundice.

questions.question: Your crew responds to a home where the family's free-roaming dogs sleep indoors covered in ticks. A child in the home has a high fever and a spotted rash and is diagnosed with Rocky Mountain spotted fever. The organism reached the child through which route?
questions.explanation: The ticks on the dogs are the animal vectors that delivered the bacteria to the child.

questions.question: After the April 19, 1995 bombing of the Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City, which killed 168 people, researchers interviewed 255 survivors about six months later. They found 45% had a postdisaster psychiatric disorder, while many others were distressed and hyperaroused without meeting criteria for an illness. What should providers expect after a critical incident?
choices: Responders who do not develop a disorder were not really affected by the event.
Only people who meet criteria for a psychiatric disorder need support after an incident.
Distress is the common response after a critical incident, so support should be normalized for all responders and survivors, not only those with a diagnosed disorder.
Distress after a disaster is a sign of poor training and should be documented as such.
questions.explanation: Distress affects far more people than those who develop a formal disorder after an incident.

questions.question: A paramedic describes her career: emergency calls once spiked her heart rate every time, then she adapted and handled them calmly, but years of chronic short staffing have left her drained and constantly fatigued. She is describing what?
questions.explanation: Alarm, then reaction and resistance, then exhaustion from prolonged stress is the general adaptation syndrome.

questions.question: Swabs from an ambulance on permanent duty found Staphylococcus aureus in over half of samples, and 40% of those isolates were MRSA, even though high-standard disinfection had been applied; the authors blamed protective biofilm and failures of technique and contact time. What must crews do for disinfectant to actually work?
choices: Apply disinfectant as directed and let surfaces air dry for the full contact time; wiping dry early or skimping coverage leaves biofilm-protected bacteria alive.
Clean only visibly soiled surfaces, since biofilm forms only where soil can be seen.
Use a weaker disinfectant solution so no residue is left on surfaces.
Wipe the disinfectant dry right away so the unit can return to service faster.
questions.explanation: Decontamination fails when technique, product choice, or contact time is wrong; surfaces need full directed contact time and air drying.

questions.question: During a routine physical, a firefighter mentions that ever since a building collapse early in his career he has flashbacks when he hears a PASS alarm and has started drinking to sleep. What delayed stress reaction is this?
questions.explanation: Flashbacks and avoidance surfacing long after a life-threatening incident are hallmarks of PTSD.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The primary federal agency that conducts and supports public health activities in the United States.
choices: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
questions.explanation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: The primary federal agency that conducts and supports public health activities in the United States.
questions.topic: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

questions.question: A new hire asks who requires your employer to offer the hepatitis B vaccine free and to provide PPE at no cost. Which agency's standard makes that mandatory?
choices: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
questions.explanation: Those duties come from OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030.

questions.question: Your service treats every patient's blood and body fluids as potentially infectious, gloves up for every IV start, and disinfects the cot after every run, no matter the diagnosis. What is this system called?
questions.explanation: Applying CDC protective measures to all patients and all body fluids is standard precautions.

questions.question: An EMT student is asked to classify a patient's illness: a virus has invaded the patient's body, is multiplying, and is producing fever and a cough. What general term describes a medical condition caused this way?
questions.explanation: The condition is produced by harmful organisms growing and spreading inside the body, which is the definition of an infectious disease.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A microorganism that is capable of causing disease in a susceptible host.
questions.explanation: pathogen: A microorganism that is capable of causing disease in a susceptible host.

questions.question: You are suctioning a bleeding airway and blood sprays toward your face. You are wearing only your prescription glasses. What PPE are you missing?
questions.explanation: Prescription glasses offer little or no side protection against splashes.

questions.question: Before 1991, occupational bloodborne exposures were estimated to cause more than 200 deaths and 9,000 infections a year; after a new federal standard took effect, reported occupational hepatitis B infections among healthcare workers fell from about 8,700 in 1987 to about 800 in 1995. A new EMT asks why your service has a written exposure control plan, sharps containers, and free hepatitis B vaccination. What is the correct answer?
choices: They exist because OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard mandates exposure control plans, PPE, and free hepatitis B vaccination.
They are voluntary courtesy benefits the service offers, with no legal requirement behind them.
They come from a state law that applies only to hospitals, not ambulance services.
CDC requires them as a condition of the service receiving Medicare reimbursement.
questions.explanation: Your exposure control plan, sharps containers, and free hepatitis B shots exist because OSHA mandates them.

questions.question: What does the term "infection" mean?
choices: Reactions to stress that occur after a stressful situation.
The primary federal agency that conducts and supports public health activities in the United States.
The organism or individual that is attacked by the infecting agent.
The abnormal invasion of a host or host tissues by organisms such as bacteria, viruses, or parasites, with or without signs or symptoms of disease.
questions.explanation: infection: The abnormal invasion of a host or host tissues by organisms such as bacteria, viruses, or parasites, with or without signs or symptoms of disease.

questions.question: After Hurricane Ian flooded Lee and Collier Counties, Florida in 2022, 29 people developed Vibrio vulnificus infections through wounds exposed to floodwater, and 11 died. What should responders do when working around floodwater?
choices: Wounds exposed to floodwater should be sealed under an occlusive dressing and not checked for several days.
Only deep puncture wounds can become infected in floodwater, so minor cuts need no attention.
Cover wounds before floodwater work and watch any wound exposed to floodwater closely for infection.
Floodwater dilutes bacteria enough that exposed wounds can safely be left uncovered.
questions.explanation: Cover wounds before floodwater work and watch any wound exposed to floodwater closely for infection.

questions.question: Congress passed the Ryan White CARE Act in 1990. Its responder provisions required emergency response employers to name a designated officer for exposure questions, and hospitals were required to tell that officer whether a source patient had a listed infectious disease. Why does this designated officer role matter?
choices: The designated officer personally treats every exposed provider at the hospital.
The designated officer is the department's official channel for exposure notification, which is what makes hospitals share source-patient results with the agency.
The designated officer role exists mainly to discipline providers who skip PPE.
Any crew member can call the hospital directly and get a source patient's test results.
questions.explanation: Exposure follow-up runs through the designated officer, the person charged with managing exposures and infection control.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A sexually transmitted infectious disease caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum; unlike many infections, it confers no protection from reinfection after exposure, so a treated person can catch it again.
questions.explanation: syphilis: A sexually transmitted infectious disease caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum; unlike many infections, it confers no protection from reinfection after exposure, so a treated person can catch it again.

questions.question: What does the term "syphilis" mean?
choices: Handling needles and other sharps carefully and disposing of them properly; careless handling of sharps is the usual route by which HIV and hepatitis are spread in health care settings.

A sexually transmitted infectious disease caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum; unlike many infections, it confers no protection from reinfection after exposure, so a treated person can catch it again.
The use of objects to limit a person's ability to see you.

What are the hazards at a structure fire that include possible building collapse, high heat, smoke and toxic gases, and oxygen-deficient air, and that require EMTs to stage at a safe distance and stay clear until the fire department declares the scene safe.
questions.explanation: syphilis: A sexually transmitted infectious disease caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum; unlike many infections, it confers no protection from reinfection after exposure, so a treated person can catch it again.

questions.question: At Vienna General Hospital in 1847, mothers in the doctors' clinic died of childbed fever at far higher rates than in the midwives' clinic. Ignaz Semmelweis ordered handwashing in chlorinated lime solution after autopsy work, and mortality fell from 18.3% in April to 2.2% in June and 1.2% in July. What does this founding case establish?
choices: Hand hygiene is the single most effective infection control step on every call.
Mortality fell because the midwives' clinic admitted healthier patients, not because of handwashing.
Handwashing matters only after autopsy or morgue work, not between patients.
Gloves make hand hygiene unnecessary when they are changed between patients.
questions.explanation: One simple procedure — disinfecting hands between patients — cut deaths dramatically: the founding demonstration of infection control.

questions.question: After transporting a patient with influenza, the crew disinfects all contact surfaces and launders the linens before returning to service. This routine is part of which practice?
questions.explanation: Cleaning and disinfecting after a contagious patient is a core infection control procedure.

questions.question: During the COVID-19 pandemic, a Spanish study of 506 healthcare professionals used the ProQOL scale to measure professional quality of life after months of caring for dying patients. It found 60.4% of respondents had high levels of compassion fatigue and another 33.6% had moderate levels. What pattern does this case show?
choices: Compassion fatigue develops gradually as compassion erodes over months of caring for suffering patients, and it should be treated as a measurable occupational injury, not an attitude problem.
Compassion fatigue is a sudden reaction to one especially bad call.
High compassion fatigue scores simply mean the clinicians chose the wrong profession.
Only new, inexperienced clinicians are at risk of losing compassion for patients.
questions.explanation: Compassion fatigue is the gradual lessening of compassion over time with sustained caregiving.

questions.question: A nursing home reports several residents ill after a virus spread through the dining hall. In the incident report, that virus is documented as which type of agent?
questions.explanation: The virus is the disease-causing microorganism in this outbreak, which is exactly what pathogen means.

questions.question: An EMT who once volunteered for every community event now feels emotionally numb, snaps at frequent-flyer patients, and is making documentation errors after two years of short staffing and back-to-back shifts. His supervisor should recognize which condition?
questions.explanation: His detachment and cynicism, exhaustion, and declining work quality all grew out of chronic job stress, matching burnout rather than a single bad call.

questions.question: In July 1976, attendees of the American Legion convention at a Philadelphia hotel developed a severe, mysterious pneumonia; 182 people became ill and 29 died. Investigators eventually found a previously unknown bacterium, Legionella pneumophila, breeding in the hotel's air-conditioning cooling tower and spreading through the building in water droplets. What is the key lesson for an EMT who notices several patients with severe pneumonia tied to the same building?
choices: The crew should enter the building's mechanical areas to inspect the cooling tower themselves before reporting anything.
Clusters of severe pneumonia linked to one building or water system should be reported early, because the pattern is the clue to the organism.
Each pneumonia patient should be treated as an isolated case, since patients from the same building rarely share a cause.
Patients should be told the illness is most likely a common cold virus and does not need follow-up.
questions.explanation: The Legionnaires' outbreak was solved by recognizing the pattern of cases linked to one building, so early reporting of clusters is the clue to the organism.

questions.question: During the 2003 season, five St. Louis Rams players developed MRSA infections, and every infection started at a turf-burn abrasion, mostly in linemen and linebackers; investigators blamed skin-to-skin contact, shared towels, and communal whirlpools. What precaution does this case stress for an EMT?
choices: Cover your own broken skin before patient contact, because open cuts are a doorway for infection.
Abrasions should be left uncovered so they can dry out during the shift.
Skin infections like MRSA spread only through the air, so covering cuts does not matter.
Gloves alone are enough protection even when the EMT has open cuts on the hands.
questions.explanation: MRSA moved between players through skin-to-skin contact at open abrasions — textbook direct contact transmission.

questions.question: In 2007, an Atlanta man with drug-resistant tuberculosis flew on international flights, exposing fellow passengers in the enclosed cabin, and the CDC issued its first federal isolation order since 1963 after he re-entered the United States. Which precaution set matches the risk he posed to people sharing his air?
choices: Mask the suspected TB patient, wear a fit-tested respirator yourself, and notify the receiving hospital and public health authorities.
Wear gloves and a surgical mask, since drug-resistant TB spreads by contact with skin and surfaces.
Isolate only after a laboratory confirms drug resistance, which can take several weeks.
Open the vehicle windows and skip respirators, because moving air eliminates the airborne risk.
questions.explanation: A suspected TB patient gets masked, the EMT wears a fit-tested respirator, and the hospital and public health authorities are notified.

questions.question: A study swabs your ambulance and finds staph bacteria on the stretcher rails and work counter even though the unit was 'cleaned' that morning. Which process most likely failed?
questions.explanation: Research repeatedly finds pathogens surviving in ambulances when cleaning and disinfection are rushed or incomplete.

questions.question: In 2010, a girls' soccer team's index case vomited in a hotel bathroom where an open reusable grocery bag of snacks was stored. Teammates who touched the bag or ate the snacks became ill with norovirus without ever touching the sick player, and the bag later tested positive. What practice does this support?
choices: Objects only transmit disease while they are still visibly wet with body fluids.
Norovirus can only spread by direct skin-to-skin contact with the sick person.
Keep food and personal items out of patient care areas, and treat shared objects as possible carriers of disease.
Food stored near a sick person is safe to share once the person has left the room.
questions.explanation: Keep food and personal items out of patient care areas, and treat shared objects as possible carriers of disease.

questions.question: Your service is cited after an inspection finds medics routinely recapping needles and no written exposure control plan. Which federal agency issued the citation?
choices: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health
questions.explanation: OSHA is the federal agency that publishes and enforces employee-safety rules, including the bloodborne pathogens standard.

questions.question: A responder screened normal one month after a disaster but screens positive for PTSD at a one-year follow-up. Which category fits?
questions.explanation: Onset after the situation, not during it, makes it delayed rather than acute.

questions.question: A choir member with COVID-19 sings indoors for 2.5 hours and most of the room later tests positive, even people who never touched him. Which term describes how this disease spread?
questions.explanation: The pathogen moved from host to others through the air; that route of spread is transmission.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (4-year-old girl in cardiac arrest): How can you help your partner?
choices: Tell him that crying on duty is unprofessional and that he needs to put the call behind him before the next shift.

Listen, offer support, and do not force him to talk. Encourage him to talk when ready, suggest debriefing or peer support, recognize signs of stress, encourage professional help if needed, be patient, and follow up with him.
Give him space and do not bring it up again, because talking about the call will only make his stress worse.
Take over all of his difficult calls for the next month so he is not exposed to another stressful incident.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.

questions.question: A paramedic transporting a patient sideswiped three parked vehicles at about 1 a.m., and post-crash testing required by department protocol showed he was under the influence of alcohol. What does this case require of EMS providers and their partners?
choices: Never work impaired, and never let an impaired partner drive or treat patients; intervene and notify a supervisor.
Give the provider coffee and a short rest in the cab, then let him resume driving.
Cover for the provider this once so he is not disciplined, and warn him privately not to repeat it.
Let the provider finish the shift as long as no one was hurt in the crash.
questions.explanation: On-duty impairment is a patient-safety emergency; coworkers must intervene and notify a supervisor rather than look away.

questions.question: What does the term "exposure" mean?
choices: Procedures to reduce transmission of infection among patients and health care personnel.

A delayed stress reaction to a prior incident. Often the result of one or more unresolved issues concerning the incident, and may relate to an incident that involved physical harm or the threat of physical harm.
A situation in which a person has had contact with blood, body fluids, tissues, or airborne particles and has the potential to develop a disease.
Reactions to stress that occur during a stressful situation.
questions.explanation: exposure: A situation in which a person has had contact with blood, body fluids, tissues, or airborne particles and has the potential to develop a disease.

questions.question: What does the term "critical incident stress management" mean?
choices: Protective measures that have traditionally been developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for use in dealing with objects, blood, body fluids, and other potential exposure risks of communicable disease; they are now officially referred to as standard precautions.
A process that confronts the responses to critical incidents and defuses them, directing the emergency services personnel toward physical and emotional equilibrium.
The abnormal invasion of a host or host tissues by organisms such as bacteria, viruses, or parasites, with or without signs or symptoms of disease.
A situation in which a person has had contact with blood, body fluids, tissues, or airborne particles and has the potential to develop a disease.
questions.explanation: critical incident stress management: A process that confronts the responses to critical incidents and defuses them, directing the emergency services personnel toward physical and emotional equilibrium.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Exposure or transmission of disease from one person to another by contact with a contaminated object.
questions.explanation: indirect contact: Exposure or transmission of disease from one person to another by contact with a contaminated object.

questions.question: What does the term "vector-borne transmission" mean?
choices: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is caused by HIV, which damages the cells in the body's immune system so that the body is unable to fight infection or certain cancers.
The individual in the department who is charged with the responsibility of managing exposures and infection control.
