The use of an animal to spread an organism from one person or place to another.
questions.explanation: vector-borne transmission: The use of an animal to spread an organism from one person or place to another.

questions.question: Of rubella, mumps, chickenpox, and syphilis, which disease can a patient catch again even after having it and being fully treated?
questions.explanation: Rubella, mumps, and chickenpox generally leave immunity; syphilis does not protect against reinfection.

questions.question: After a gunman killed 23 people at a cafeteria in Killeen, Texas, in 1991, the EMS workers who responded were offered a critical incident stress debriefing within 24 hours and were checked again 8 to 10 days later and at 1 month. Research on those workers linked debriefing attendance to better recovery from depression and anxiety symptoms. What does this case show an agency should do after a mass-casualty call?
choices: Offer the formal debriefing early after the call and check on responders again weeks later, not just that night.
Hold one debriefing the night of the call and consider the stress response finished once it is held.
Wait at least a month before offering any debriefing so responders have time to process on their own.
Make debriefing available only to responders who ask for it, since most recover without it.
questions.explanation: Offer the formal debriefing early after a mass-casualty call and follow up with responders weeks later, not just that night.

questions.question: In a 2010 experiment, students preparing for the GRE were told that bodily arousal during testing actually improves performance. That group scored higher on the lab GRE math section and, months later, on their real GRE. An EMT feels his heart racing before a skills test. What does this research support doing?
choices: Postpone the test until he feels fully calm, since a calm state is required for good performance.
Reframe the racing heart as fuel for performance, because viewing arousal as useful turns it toward eustress.
Suppress the arousal completely before starting, because any arousal during testing lowers scores.
Ignore the sensation and hope it passes, because mindset about arousal has no measurable effect.
questions.explanation: Telling yourself the racing heart is fuel measurably improves performance; the reframe produces eustress.

questions.question: CDC interim Ebola guidance for EMS systems and 911 centers states that any provider whose skin or mucous membranes contact a suspected Ebola patient's fluids should act immediately, and directs the provider to report the exposure to a supervisor or designated infection control officer as soon as possible. What should the exposed EMT do?
choices: Stop work at once, wash the exposed area, and report the exposure to a supervisor or the designated infection control officer as soon as possible.
Handle the follow-up personally by calling the hospital laboratory for the patient's results.
Wait to see whether the patient tests positive before reporting anything.
Finish the transport, then mention the exposure at the end of the shift if symptoms develop.
questions.explanation: After any exposure: stop, wash, and notify the designated officer immediately, not at the end of shift.

questions.question: During an active-shooter call, your rescue task force works behind a block wall while police provide security. The wall's tactical role is what?
questions.explanation: The wall is a bullet-stopping barrier protecting the team while they work: cover.

questions.question: In 2006, researchers cultured 21 ambulances in a western U.S. fleet and found 47.6% tested positive for MRSA, with contamination more often in crew work areas than in patient contact areas. What should crews do between calls?
choices: Ambulance surfaces only need cleaning when a patient was known to carry MRSA.
Disinfect the whole patient compartment, including crew work areas, between calls, not just the stretcher.
Crew work areas stay clean because patients never touch them during transport.
Only the stretcher needs disinfection, since organisms do not survive on other ambulance surfaces.
questions.explanation: Disinfect the whole patient compartment, including crew work areas, between calls, not just the stretcher.

questions.question: What does the term "aerosol-generating procedure" mean?
choices: Protective measures that have traditionally been developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for use in dealing with objects, blood, body fluids, and other potential exposure risks of communicable disease; they are now officially referred to as standard precautions.

Cleaning and disinfecting the ambulance and its equipment after a call, including allowing disinfected surfaces to air dry unless otherwise indicated in the product directions, so the unit is safe for the next patient.
The way in which an infectious disease is spread: contact, airborne, by vehicles, or by vectors.
Any airway manipulation that induces the production of aerosols that may present a risk for airborne transmission of pathogens, such as during CPR.
questions.explanation: aerosol-generating procedure: Any airway manipulation that induces the production of aerosols that may present a risk for airborne transmission of pathogens, such as during CPR.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (4-year-old girl in cardiac arrest): What is stress? How does it manifest?
choices: Stress is a sign of poor training. It manifests as an inability to perform skills, and experienced providers who are properly trained no longer experience it.
Stress is the body's response to a lack of sleep. It manifests mainly as fatigue and yawning, and it resolves as soon as the provider gets one full night of rest.
Stress is a purely emotional reaction that has no physical component. It manifests only as feelings of worry or sadness and does not change heart rate, breathing, or blood pressure.

Stress is a physical, mental, or emotional response to a stressor. The body activates the fight-or-flight response, with the sympathetic nervous system releasing adrenaline and norepinephrine, changing heart rate, breathing, pupil dilation, sweating, blood pressure, and blood flow. It can manifest physically (headaches, gastrointestinal upset, insomnia, fatigue), emotionally (anger, fear, anxiety), behaviorally (appetite changes, social withdrawal, substance abuse), or cognitively (difficulty concentrating, memory problems).
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.

questions.question: Spanish nursing assistant Teresa Romero cared for a missionary who died of Ebola in September 2014. She became the first person known to contract Ebola outside West Africa; investigators believed she touched her face with a contaminated glove while removing her protective suit. What practice does her case demand?
choices: Touching the face during removal is low risk, since the outside of the gloves stays clean during care.
Treat used PPE as contaminated waste and doff slowly and deliberately, with hand hygiene as part of the protection.
Remove PPE as fast as possible once care ends, because the danger ends when the suit comes off.
Skip hand hygiene after doffing if the gloves show no visible tears or contamination.
questions.explanation: The failure came at removal; used PPE is contaminated waste, and slow, deliberate doffing with hand hygiene is part of the protection.

questions.question: Beyond Blue's 'Answering the Call' survey collected responses from 21,014 current and former Australian police and emergency services personnel. One in three employees reported high or very high psychological distress, and employees with more than 10 years of service were almost twice as likely to experience it. What is the main lesson for EMS agencies?
choices: Distress accumulates with years of service, so agencies should measure it routinely instead of waiting for a crisis.
Because distress is a personal response, agencies have no reason to track it.
Distress only appears after a single catastrophic incident.
Distress is rare in emergency services and mainly affects new recruits.
questions.explanation: Distress, the negative response to stressors, builds with cumulative exposure over a career.

questions.question: In 1996, the CDC issued the Guideline for Isolation Precautions in Hospitals, merging universal precautions and body substance isolation into one protective baseline applied to every patient, every time. What does that baseline require of an EMT on every call?
choices: Apply full precautions only to patients with a confirmed infectious diagnosis.
Gloves can replace hand hygiene when you are rushed between back-to-back calls.
Learn the baseline cold: gloves, hand hygiene, sharps safety, and cleaning apply on every single call.
Precautions are a hospital policy and do not apply to field care in the ambulance.
questions.explanation: Standard precautions are one protective baseline for every patient, every time, in the field as well as the hospital.

questions.question: At a 1995 crash, firefighters worked on a car that had not been stabilized and whose cribbing was still on the truck; prying at the hood to reach the battery rocked the car and hurt the trapped occupant, and about 20 minutes later the undeployed airbags fired, injuring two firefighters. What sequence does this case demand before patient access?
choices: Pry the hood open first to disconnect the battery, since that makes stabilization safe.
Begin extrication immediately and stabilize the vehicle only if it starts to move.
Stabilize first, disconnect power, and respect undeployed airbags before starting patient access.
Treat undeployed airbags as harmless once the engine is shut off.
questions.explanation: An unsecured, still-powered vehicle moved during work and then injured its rescuers; stabilization and power control come first.

questions.question: What does the term "critical incident stress debriefing" mean?
choices: A beneficial response to a stressor.
The active pursuit of a state of good health.
The federal regulatory compliance agency that develops, publishes, and enforces guidelines concerning employee safety.

The formal, structured group debriefing held 24 to 72 hours after a critical incident, as part of critical incident stress management (CISM), in which the responders involved discuss the incident and their reactions to it.
questions.explanation: critical incident stress debriefing: The formal, structured group debriefing held 24 to 72 hours after a critical incident, as part of critical incident stress management (CISM), in which the responders involved discuss the incident and their reactions to it.

questions.question: You are about to intubate a coughing patient with suspected COVID-19, and your officer orders respirators and eye protection for everyone in the room. Why is intubation treated this way?
questions.explanation: Intubation manipulates the airway and produces infectious aerosols: an aerosol-generating procedure.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The simplest, yet most effective, method of preventing the spread of infectious disease: washing the hands in between patient contacts.
questions.explanation: hand washing: The simplest, yet most effective, method of preventing the spread of infectious disease: washing the hands in between patient contacts.

questions.question: During Hurricane Katrina deployments, a Disaster Medical Assistance Team treated almost 1,000 patients in three days at the Superdome, and the team's mental health member used Crisis Management Briefings and one-on-one interventions during 12-hour shifts instead of formal debriefings, matching the CISM tool to the moment. During a long deployment with no room in the schedule for a formal debriefing, what should the team do?
choices: Postpone all stress support until the deployment ends and a formal debriefing can be scheduled.
Cancel rest breaks so that full formal debriefings can fit into every shift.
Require every responder to attend a complete group debriefing after every shift.
Use short briefings and one-on-one check-ins on shift rather than waiting for a formal debriefing that may never fit the schedule.
questions.explanation: During a long deployment, use short briefings and check-ins on shift rather than waiting for a formal debriefing.

questions.question: What does the term "cold-weather clothing layers" mean?
choices: Reactions to stress that occur after a stressful situation.
The most effective way to preserve body heat when functioning in cold, wet weather — wearing at least three layers of clothing.
The abnormal invasion of a host or host tissues by organisms such as bacteria, viruses, or parasites, with or without signs or symptoms of disease.
A process that confronts the responses to critical incidents and defuses them, directing the emergency services personnel toward physical and emotional equilibrium.
questions.explanation: cold-weather clothing layers: The most effective way to preserve body heat when functioning in cold, wet weather — wearing at least three layers of clothing.

questions.question: Navigate Case Study (EMT with delayed stress after a school bus MCI): What are other signs and symptoms of ineffectively handled stress?
choices: The only reliable signs are physical ones such as headaches and fatigue; stress does not produce emotional or behavioral changes.
Signs include occasional sadness after a difficult call that resolves within a day and does not affect work, appetite, or sleep.
Physical signs include increased energy, improved appetite, and deeper sleep. Emotional signs include greater patience, optimism, and a stronger desire to socialize with coworkers.

Physical signs include headaches, gastrointestinal upset, insomnia, fatigue, and changes in appetite. Emotional and behavioral signs include irritability, anger, anxiety, depression, social withdrawal, difficulty concentrating, increased risk-taking, and alcohol or drug abuse.
questions.explanation: Answer written from the chapter (no printed key).

questions.question: At an apartment fire, a firefighter warns that air inside a burned room may not support life even where flames are out, and victims are coughing from carbon monoxide and other gases in the smoke. What are these dangers collectively called?
questions.explanation: Smoke carries toxic gases and displaces oxygen, creating an oxygen-deficient atmosphere.

questions.question: Before a difficult extrication, an EMT feels her heart rate climb and her focus sharpen. She performs better than usual and later says the pressure 'got her locked in.' What is this beneficial response to a stressor called?
questions.explanation: The stressor improved her performance instead of harming it, which is the definition of eustress.

questions.question: In 1993, E. coli O157:H7 in undercooked hamburger patties from Jack in the Box restaurants sickened 732 people across four western states. Four children died and 178 people were left with permanent injury, including kidney and brain damage. What is the key lesson for EMTs from this outbreak?
choices: Clusters of bloody diarrhea in children after eating out should be reported quickly, because early recognition of foodborne transmission helps stop outbreaks.
Undercooked food only causes mild illness, so clusters of cases do not need urgent reporting.
Bloody diarrhea after a meal is usually caused by airborne spread inside the restaurant.
Food histories are not useful on GI calls because hospitals identify outbreaks on their own.
questions.explanation: Contaminated food is a classic vehicle for foodborne transmission, and clusters are the clue that links cases into an outbreak.

questions.question: An officer tells you a patrol car's door panel will not stop rifle fire, but the concrete planter will. Moving behind the planter is choosing what?
questions.explanation: The planter is an impenetrable barrier used for protection: cover.

questions.question: What does the term "eustress" mean?
choices: Exposure or transmission of disease from one person to another by contact with a contaminated object.
A beneficial response to a stressor.
The federal regulatory compliance agency that develops, publishes, and enforces guidelines concerning employee safety.
The capacity of an individual to cope with and recover from distress.
questions.explanation: eustress: A beneficial response to a stressor.

questions.question: A toddler at daycare mouths a toy that a child sick with norovirus drooled on an hour earlier, and she becomes ill. She never touched the sick child. This is an example of what?
questions.explanation: The toy acted as the contaminated object carrying the virus from one child to the other.

questions.question: At the 2017 Route 91 Harvest festival shooting in Las Vegas, a gunman fired from the 32nd floor of a hotel into the crowd, killing about 60 people. Crews had to treat and move patients while the shooter overlooked the venue. What is the best action?
choices: Move patients behind vehicles and structures that block the shooter's line of sight, and use any available vehicle to get them out.
Set up a treatment area in the open center of the venue so all patients are in one visible place.
Wait inside the venue without moving patients until every floor of the hotel is fully cleared.
Stand rescuers in a group around each patient to shield the patient with their bodies.
questions.explanation: In a mass shooting, move patients behind concealment fast and use any available vehicle to get them out.

questions.question: CDC surveyed New Orleans police officers and firefighters 7–13 weeks after Hurricane Katrina struck in August 2005. Of 525 firefighters, 22% reported PTSD symptoms and 27% reported major depressive symptoms, and many responders had also lost their own homes in the flooding. What operational lesson does this support?
choices: Personal losses at home do not affect a responder's stress level on duty.
Rest rotations can be suspended during disasters because the work itself builds resilience.
Rotate crews and protect rest during long disasters; responders who are also victims need extra support.
Responders who lost homes should be kept on duty longer to keep their minds off their losses.
questions.explanation: Weeks of disaster duty while personally displaced is prolonged, excessive stress — the recipe for cumulative stress reactions.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The use of objects to limit a person's ability to see you.
questions.explanation: concealment: The use of objects to limit a person's ability to see you.

questions.question: After September 11, FDNY screened 8,487 firefighters; although 76% reported at least one symptom, 2,389 firefighters (28%) self-referred to the department's Counseling Services Unit, a five-fold increase over pre-9/11 use, and most remained on the job and recovered. A firefighter who hesitates to use that counseling because he thinks it looks weak should understand what?
choices: He should rely only on time off and avoid talking about the incident with anyone.
Using peer and counseling support early is part of resilience, not a sign of weakness.
Using counseling marks a responder as unfit and should be avoided after catastrophic calls.
He should wait at least a year before using counseling so natural recovery can happen first.
questions.explanation: Using peer and counseling support early is part of resilience, not a sign of weakness.

questions.question: Researchers cultured five sites in each of 21 ambulances and found MRSA in nearly half the fleet; the work area beside the patient was the most contaminated site, and MRSA was also recovered from stretcher handrails, cushions, steering wheels, and suction tips. What does this study require of crews cleaning up after a call?
choices: Disinfect only the stretcher, since that is the only surface the patient touches.
Skip the steering wheel and work counter, because patients never touch them.
Decontaminate the whole patient compartment, including crew work areas, not just the stretcher.
Accept that MRSA in ambulances is unavoidable, so a quick wipe-down is sufficient.
questions.explanation: Routine cleaning was leaving MRSA throughout working ambulances, so the whole compartment, including work areas, must be decontaminated.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Handling needles and other sharps carefully and disposing of them properly; careless handling of sharps is the usual route by which HIV and hepatitis are spread in health care settings.
questions.explanation: sharps safety: Handling needles and other sharps carefully and disposing of them properly; careless handling of sharps is the usual route by which HIV and hepatitis are spread in health care settings.

questions.question: Blood from a trauma patient splashes into an EMT's eyes. She feels fine and has no symptoms, but the hospital still sends her to occupational health. What has she had, by definition?
questions.explanation: Contact with blood or body fluids with the potential to develop disease is an exposure, even before any illness appears.

questions.question: Assessment in Action: What are the long-term physical effects of stress?
choices: Long-term physical effects of stress include night sweats, a productive cough, fever, and unexplained weight loss.
Long-term physical effects of stress include improved immune function, increased energy, better sleep, and a lower resting heart rate.
Long-term physical effects of stress are limited to temporary muscle tension and mild headaches that resolve within a few days.
Long-term physical effects of stress include changes in appetite, gastrointestinal problems, backache, headaches, and fatigue.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed answer key.

questions.question: You arrive at a rollover with the car resting on its side and a patient trapped inside. Your partner wants to climb in through the rear window immediately. What must happen first?
questions.explanation: The vehicle must be stabilized with struts or cribbing before anyone accesses the patient, or it may roll or drop onto both of you.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The presence of infectious organisms on or in objects such as dressings, water, food, needles, wounds, or a patient's body.
questions.explanation: contamination: The presence of infectious organisms on or in objects such as dressings, water, food, needles, wounds, or a patient's body.

questions.question: During the 2014 Dallas Ebola response, the PPE worn by nurses caring for patient Thomas Eric Duncan left areas of the neck exposed, and two nurses became infected. The CDC then revised its guidance to require full coverage with no skin showing and a trained observer for doffing. What is the lesson for an EMT donning PPE?
choices: PPE is only as good as its weakest gap, and removal is the most dangerous step, so use a buddy check when doffing.
A small area of exposed skin is acceptable as long as the respirator and gloves fit correctly.
Doffing quickly is safest, because speed reduces the time spent near contaminated equipment.
Once the patient is stabilized, PPE gaps no longer matter because the exposure window has passed.
questions.explanation: One exposed gap defeats the whole barrier; removal is the most dangerous step and needs a buddy check.

questions.question: What does the term "compassion fatigue" mean?
choices: A situation in which a person has had contact with blood, body fluids, tissues, or airborne particles and has the potential to develop a disease.
What airborne bacterial disease is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spreads when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and is indicated by a positive skin test showing exposure to the bacterium.
A stress disorder characterized by gradual lessening of compassion over time.
A microorganism that is capable of causing disease in a susceptible host.
questions.explanation: compassion fatigue: A stress disorder characterized by gradual lessening of compassion over time.

questions.question: What does the term "foodborne transmission" mean?
choices: The organism or individual that is attacked by the infecting agent.
The active pursuit of a state of good health.
The abnormal invasion of a host or host tissues by organisms such as bacteria, viruses, or parasites, with or without signs or symptoms of disease.
The contamination of food or water with an organism that can cause disease.
questions.explanation: foodborne transmission: The contamination of food or water with an organism that can cause disease.

questions.question: A patient with hepatitis C is bleeding heavily from a leg wound. Your partner reminds you to glove up and watch for splashes because the virus travels in blood. What is hepatitis C classified as?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis C is a pathogenic microorganism present in human blood that can cause disease in humans, a bloodborne pathogen.

questions.question: At the 2003 Station nightclub fire in Rhode Island, pyrotechnics ignited flammable foam and 100 people died. Investigators found toxic, superheated smoke filled the building in about 90 seconds, with oxygen falling below 12 percent and carbon monoxide and hydrogen cyanide passing tenability limits in the same span. How should EMTs set up at a fire like this?
choices: Send EMTs in pairs for quick interior sweeps during the first two minutes, before conditions worsen.
Focus on burn treatment only, since smoke conditions inside assembly buildings are rarely lethal.
Expect rapid smoke-inhalation and burn casualties and set up treatment outside the hazard zone.
Set up the treatment area just inside the main entrance, where victims can reach it fastest.
questions.explanation: Extreme heat, toxic gases, and oxygen deficiency make a fire's interior unsurvivable in minutes, so treatment is set up outside the hazard zone.

questions.question: A firefighter-paramedic on months of mandatory overtime first feels keyed up on every call, then seems to cope, then develops constant fatigue, insomnia, and frequent colds as his body wears down. This progression is an example of what?
questions.explanation: The staged progression from alarm through resistance to exhaustion is the body's general adaptation syndrome.

questions.question: An EMT recaps a used needle with two hands before throwing it away, 'to make it safe.' Why is this against sharps safety practice?
questions.explanation: Recapping is a leading cause of needlesticks; used sharps should be dropped directly into a sharps container, never recapped.

questions.question: A compounding pharmacy in Massachusetts shipped steroid injections contaminated with fungus, causing 753 cases of fungal meningitis and 64 deaths across 20 states after the medication was injected into patients' spines and joints. What is the EMT's takeaway from this case?
choices: Filter any cloudy medication through gauze to remove contaminants before administering it.
Never use a medication that looks off or is past date, and report suspect products immediately.
Only hospital staff need to worry about contaminated medications; EMS products are always sterile.
Inject the medication anyway if the patient is critical, since contamination is rarely harmful.
questions.explanation: A medication that should have been sterile carried living fungus, so suspect or expired products must never be used.

questions.question: During a long ice-rescue standby, a crew member removes his insulating middle layer because he feels warm while working, then becomes chilled and clumsy once he stops moving. What protective practice did he break?
choices: a windbreaker over a uniform shirt
questions.explanation: Layering lets you add or remove layers with activity level so you stay warm without sweating through your insulation.

questions.question: In 1997 the IAFF and IAFC launched the Fire Service Joint Labor Management Wellness-Fitness Initiative, built together by ten metropolitan departments and their unions, including FDNY, Seattle, Phoenix, and LA County. The program is mandatory in structure but non-punitive, covering medical exams, fitness, rehabilitation, and behavioral health. What makes this wellness model work?
choices: Wellness works when labor and management build the program together and keep it non-punitive, as an organized, career-long pursuit of good health.
A wellness program only needs to cover fitness testing once, at hiring.
Wellness is an individual responsibility, so departments should not organize programs.
Wellness programs work best when failing a fitness test leads to discipline.
questions.explanation: Wellness is the active pursuit of good health, best pursued as an organized, non-punitive system.

questions.question: In March 2020, a choir in Skagit County, Washington held a 2.5-hour practice with 61 people, including one symptomatic singer. Afterward 53 people became ill with COVID-19, most without close contact with the singer. What is the main lesson for EMS crews?
choices: Long time spent in a closed room with an airborne illness is high risk even without close contact with the patient.
Brief calls are the highest airborne risk, while long enclosed exposures add little danger.
A patient who is not coughing during transport cannot contaminate the air of an enclosed space.
Airborne illness only spreads within 6 feet, so distance alone in a closed room is complete protection.
questions.explanation: Long time in a closed room with an airborne illness is high risk even without close contact with the patient.

questions.question: In rural Scott County, Indiana, a county that had seen about five HIV cases in the previous decade saw an explosive outbreak in 2015 among people injecting the painkiller Opana ER with shared syringes; 188 cases were confirmed by April 2016, and over 90% of patients also had hepatitis C. What should an EMT take from this outbreak?
choices: A patient who injects drugs should be refused transport until they agree to HIV testing.
HIV outbreaks only occur in large cities, so rural crews do not need sharps precautions.
Used needles found at a scene are safe to handle once the patient has been loaded.
Assume any shared needle or blood exposure can carry HIV, and report sharps injuries immediately.
questions.explanation: HIV can spread silently through shared syringes and blood, so every sharps exposure must be treated as a risk and reported at once.

questions.question: Your crew arrives first at a warehouse fire with heavy fire showing. No fire apparatus is on scene yet and bystanders urge you to go inside for a trapped worker. Why do you stage away from the building and wait?
questions.explanation: An unstable, superheated, smoke-filled structure can collapse or flash over; entry is a fire department operation.

questions.question: After the United Airlines Flight 232 crash in Sioux City killed 111 people, debriefings were offered to responders and victim-identification workers, but unprepared teenage morgue volunteers developed acute critical incident stress and needed months of therapy; the formal recommendation afterward was that critical incident stress teams be called in during and after disasters. What is the lesson for your service?
choices: Screen and prepare everyone exposed to the dead, including volunteers, and bring the stress team in early.
Send volunteers home without follow-up, since stress services only cover employees.
Reserve stress support for uniformed responders and keep volunteers out of the debriefings.
Wait until volunteers start missing shifts before offering them any stress support.
questions.explanation: Everyone exposed to the dead, including volunteers, should be screened, prepared, and supported by the stress team early.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A stress disorder characterized by gradual lessening of compassion over time.
questions.explanation: compassion fatigue: A stress disorder characterized by gradual lessening of compassion over time.

questions.question: Shots are fired at a scene. Your partner ducks behind the engine block of the ambulance while you move a patient behind a concrete pillar that stops bullets. What are you using?
questions.explanation: A barrier that actually stops rounds is cover, not mere concealment.

questions.question: Your partner arrives for shift smelling of alcohol, slurring words, and stumbling, but insists he is fine to drive the ambulance. What is this situation an example of?
questions.explanation: Working while impaired by alcohol is substance abuse and puts the patient, the crew, and the public at risk.

questions.question: After wading through floodwater with an open leg cut, a patient develops a rapidly spreading bacterial invasion of the tissue with fever and severe pain. This condition is best described as what?
questions.explanation: Bacteria entered through the cut and invaded the host tissue, which is an infection.

questions.question: A new EMT's first major trauma call triggers a surge of adrenaline. Over the next months he learns to stay steady under pressure, but after two years of nonstop overtime with no recovery he is burned out, exhausted, and sick often. This alarm, resistance, then exhaustion pattern is called what?
questions.explanation: His body moved through the alarm response and resistance stage, then hit exhaustion when the stress never let up.

questions.question: A paramedic's ungloved hand touches a patient's bloody laceration while controlling bleeding. If the patient carries hepatitis B, the paramedic's risk came through which route?
questions.explanation: Physical contact with the patient's blood is transmission by direct contact.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The abnormal invasion of a host or host tissues by organisms such as bacteria, viruses, or parasites, with or without signs or symptoms of disease.
questions.explanation: infection: The abnormal invasion of a host or host tissues by organisms such as bacteria, viruses, or parasites, with or without signs or symptoms of disease.

questions.question: Assessment in Action: Discuss the implications of your partner’s actions in this scenario.
choices: Your partner's actions carry no real risk, because a single brief exposure to a patient with tuberculosis almost never results in infection.
Your partner's actions affect only the patient, who may need to be isolated at the hospital until test results are available.

Your partner’s sloppiness in failing to take standard precautions may adversely impact his health and the health of his family. Specifically, he may become exposed to an airborne disease that he could spread to others, including his coworkers, his patients, and his own family.
Your partner's actions are mainly a documentation problem, since the exposure only matters if it is not recorded on the patient care report.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed answer key.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (4-year-old girl in cardiac arrest): Does death of a child affect an EMT differently than death of an adult? If so, how?
choices: No. Providers are trained to treat every death the same, and the age of the patient does not change the emotional response.

The death of a child is often more emotional and more difficult to cope with than the death of an adult. It can trigger personal identification with the child or family and feelings of grief, guilt, and a sense of failure, and it can be harder to accept because a child has not had a chance to live a full life.
A child's death affects an EMT less, because pediatric calls are rare and providers have little time to form any attachment.
The death of an adult is usually harder, because adults have families and responsibilities that children do not yet have.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.

questions.question: Your patient has active tuberculosis and coughs throughout transport, filling the closed ambulance with dried respiratory particles that drift in the air. The spread of an organism this way is called what?
questions.explanation: TB spreads when organisms travel through the air on droplets or dust and are inhaled.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The body's ability to protect itself from acquiring a disease.
questions.explanation: immune: The body's ability to protect itself from acquiring a disease.

questions.question: At the Endoscopy Center of Southern Nevada in 2008, staff reused syringes and single-dose medication vials between patients. About 50,000 patients were notified and urged to test for hepatitis C, hepatitis B, and HIV, and nine hepatitis C infections were genetically confirmed as clinic-linked. What rule does this case make absolute?
choices: Single-dose vials can be shared between patients if the top is wiped with alcohol.
Reusing injection equipment is acceptable when supplies are running low.
A syringe may be reused on the same patient if the needle is changed each time.
One syringe, one needle, one vial entry — never reuse injection equipment.
questions.explanation: Skipping basic infection control procedures turned a routine clinic into one of the largest exposure events in US history.

questions.question: A large STD center reviewed its syphilis cases over nine years and found that of 1,859 episodes in 663 patients, 55.5% were reinfections rather than first infections, and the authors state that syphilis infection does not confer definitive, protective immunity. What should providers expect and advise?
choices: Assume most repeat episodes mean the first infection was never actually treated.
Expect reinfection only in patients whose HIV is untreated.
Expect repeat infections in at-risk patients and encourage follow-up testing after any treatment.
Advise treated patients that one infection protects them against catching syphilis again.
questions.explanation: Catching syphilis again was more common than catching it the first time; the disease leaves no protective immunity.

questions.question: Three days after a dog bite, your patient's wound is red, swollen, warm, and draining pus as bacteria multiply in the tissue. This abnormal invasion of tissue by organisms is called what?
questions.explanation: Bacteria invading and multiplying in the wound tissue is an infection.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (4-year-old girl in cardiac arrest): What phase of the stress response are you experiencing right now?
choices: The alarm phase, the first phase of the general adaptation syndrome: the body reacts to the stressor, the fight-or-flight response is activated, and the shaking hands, rapid breathing, and racing heart are symptoms.
The exhaustion phase, the final phase of the general adaptation syndrome: the body's resources are depleted after prolonged exposure to the stressor.
A delayed stress reaction, in which symptoms such as shaking hands and a racing heart appear days to weeks after the incident ends.
The resistance phase, the second phase of the general adaptation syndrome: the body has adapted to the stressor and vital signs have returned to normal.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.

questions.question: What does the term "cumulative stress reactions" mean?
choices: A beneficial response to a stressor.
The body's ability to protect itself from acquiring a disease.

Protective measures that have traditionally been developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for use in dealing with objects, blood, body fluids, and other potential exposure risks of communicable disease; they are now officially referred to as standard precautions.
questions.explanation: cumulative stress reactions: Prolonged or excessive stress.

questions.question: A veteran EMT notices that over the past year she has stopped introducing herself to patients, feels irritated by minor complaints, and no longer feels anything when a patient cries. Her empathy has slowly drained away. What is this called?
questions.explanation: The gradual loss of compassion after repeated exposure to others' suffering is the defining feature of compassion fatigue.

questions.question: A new EMT asks why she washes hands and changes gloves between two patients who both 'look healthy.' What principle is she following?
questions.explanation: Standard precautions assume any patient can carry a communicable disease, diagnosed or not.

questions.question: What does the term "quid pro quo" mean?
choices: The body's response to stress that begins with an alarm response, followed by a stage of reaction and resistance, and then recovery or, if the stress is prolonged, exhaustion.
What type of sexual harassment occurs when the harasser requests sexual favors in exchange for something else, such as a promotion, a job benefit, a better shift, or a favorable evaluation.
What airborne bacterial disease is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spreads when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and is indicated by a positive skin test showing exposure to the bacterium.
The active pursuit of a state of good health.
questions.explanation: quid pro quo: What type of sexual harassment occurs when the harasser requests sexual favors in exchange for something else, such as a promotion, a job benefit, a better shift, or a favorable evaluation.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The capacity of an individual to cope with and recover from distress.
questions.explanation: resilience: The capacity of an individual to cope with and recover from distress.

questions.question: On May 14, 1796, Edward Jenner inoculated 8-year-old James Phipps with cowpox material from a dairymaid. When Jenner deliberately exposed the boy to smallpox weeks later, Phipps did not develop the disease. What principle did this first vaccination demonstrate?
choices: Immunity only develops after a person survives the actual disease, never from a milder related infection.
Vaccination works by treating an active infection after symptoms have already appeared.
Immunity can be built before exposure, which is the entire basis of the vaccines EMTs are required to keep current.
Prior exposure offers no real protection, so the boy's recovery was simply a matter of chance.
questions.explanation: Immunity can be built before exposure; that is the basis of vaccination.

questions.question: After a brutal month of calls, your partner still shows up steady, talks through hard runs with the crew, and returns to baseline instead of burning out. What protective capacity is she demonstrating?
questions.explanation: Recovering to normal function after repeated stressors is resilience in action.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (4-year-old girl in cardiac arrest): How can poorly managed stress affect your physical well-being?
choices: Poorly managed stress mainly causes minor, temporary complaints such as tension headaches that resolve with a single day off.
Poorly managed stress affects only mood and sleep; it does not change the immune system or the risk of any disease.
Poorly managed stress has no lasting physical effects, because the body fully recovers once the stressful shift ends.

Prolonged or poorly managed stress can cause a variety of physical symptoms and deplete the body, weakening the immune system and increasing the risk of heart disease, hypertension, cancer, alcoholism, and drug abuse.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.

questions.question: In 1847, a maternity clinic where doctors came straight from autopsies lost about 18% of mothers to childbed fever. When the physician in charge required hand disinfection with chlorinated lime solution before examining patients, mortality fell to about 2% within two months, with no other major change. What does this case demonstrate?
choices: Isolating fever patients in a separate ward is what actually ended the deaths.
Deliveries are safest when handled only by midwives rather than physicians.
Disinfecting instruments and bedding matters more than disinfecting hands.
Hand hygiene between patient contacts is a proven infection-control intervention that dramatically reduces patient deaths.
questions.explanation: Hand hygiene is the original, proven infection-control intervention; deaths collapsed when hands were disinfected between contacts.

questions.question: A cook carries typhoid bacteria in her gallbladder for years without ever feeling sick, while the bacteria live off her body. What is she, biologically, to those bacteria?
questions.explanation: She is the organism the infecting agent lives in, a host, even though she has no symptoms.

questions.question: After a 1989 earthquake in Newcastle, Australia, researchers followed 195 disaster helpers for 2 years, comparing 62 who were debriefed with 133 who were not. They found no evidence that the debriefed helpers recovered any faster, even after exposure level was taken into account. What is the correct lesson for an EMS agency?
choices: Stop offering debriefings entirely, since this study proves they have no value for responders.
Replace group debriefings with a single written stress survey mailed out a year after the incident.
Do not treat a debriefing as a guarantee against PTSD; keep watching responders over time and refer those who are struggling.
Assume any responder who attended a debriefing is cleared of PTSD risk and needs no follow-up.
questions.explanation: A debriefing is not a guarantee against PTSD; monitor responders over time and refer those who struggle.

questions.question: At a summer camp, dozens of children become ill with bloody diarrhea after eating undercooked burgers at a cookout. Investigators trace the bacteria to the ground beef. How was the organism transmitted?
questions.explanation: The pathogen reached the patients through contaminated food, the definition of foodborne transmission.

questions.question: A paramedic repeatedly takes fentanyl from the ambulance narcotics box, refills the vials with saline, and documents doses that were never given. A trauma patient later gets no pain relief from a vial that should have contained fentanyl. What provider problem caused this patient harm?
questions.explanation: Diverting narcotics for personal use is substance abuse, and patients who receive saline instead of medication get substandard care.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A medical condition caused by the growth and spread of small, harmful organisms within the body.
questions.explanation: infectious disease: A medical condition caused by the growth and spread of small, harmful organisms within the body.

questions.question: What does the term "bloodborne pathogens" mean?
choices: Pathogenic microorganisms that are present in human blood and can cause disease in humans. These pathogens include, but are not limited to, hepatitis B virus and human immunodeficiency virus.
The capacity of an individual to cope with and recover from distress.
A microorganism that is capable of causing disease in a susceptible host.
The individual in the department who is charged with the responsibility of managing exposures and infection control.
questions.explanation: bloodborne pathogens: Pathogenic microorganisms that are present in human blood and can cause disease in humans. These pathogens include, but are not limited to, hepatitis B virus and human immunodeficiency virus.

questions.question: What does the term "immune" mean?
choices: The body's ability to protect itself from acquiring a disease.
A combination of exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced performance resulting from long-term job stresses.
The use of objects to limit a person's ability to see you.
A beneficial response to a stressor.
questions.explanation: immune: The body's ability to protect itself from acquiring a disease.

questions.question: During decon, an EMT asks why the ambulance must be disinfected after every patient, not just visibly sick ones. The answer is to kill any disease-causing microorganism that may be present. That microorganism is a what?
questions.explanation: Disinfection targets pathogens — microorganisms capable of causing disease — whether or not illness is obvious.

questions.question: An EMT starts a station routine of exercising on shift, keeping regular sleep hours on days off, getting an annual physical, and attending a peer support night each month. What concept is she practicing?
questions.explanation: Wellness is the active pursuit of good health, and her routine deliberately pursues physical and mental health.

questions.question: Your department replaces a punitive fitness test with voluntary health screenings, nutrition coaching, and on-duty workout time, aiming to keep crews healthy across a whole career. What is the program's focus?
questions.explanation: The program actively pursues a state of good health rather than just treating illness or injury.

questions.question: After a line-of-duty death, your department brings in a trained peer team for a defusing that night, a structured group debriefing two days later, and follow-up check-ins. This whole organized process is known as what?
questions.explanation: Defusings, debriefings, and follow-up are the components of CISM, the process that moves responders back toward equilibrium.

questions.question: In a landmark Supreme Court case, a bank employee alleged her supervisor forced her into sex repeatedly and that she submitted out of fear of losing her job. The Court held that sexual harassment is sex discrimination under Title VII and recognized quid pro quo harassment. What makes a supervisor's sexual demands coercive in this pattern?
choices: Sexual demands are only coercive if the supervisor states a specific threat in front of witnesses.
The conduct only counts as harassment if it happens during scheduled work hours at the workplace.
A supervisor's job power makes sexual demands coercive, even without an explicit threat spoken aloud.
A supervisor's demands are not harassment as long as the employee is never actually fired.
questions.explanation: A supervisor's power over the job makes sexual demands coercive even without an explicit threat.

questions.question: A patient with advanced HIV is transported with pneumonia that a healthy person would normally fight off. The pneumonia is dangerous mainly because which virus has damaged his immune defenses?
questions.explanation: HIV weakens the immune system over time, so ordinary infections can become life-threatening.

questions.question: During her review, an EMT's supervisor says her evaluation will improve if she sends him explicit photos, and will suffer if she refuses. What is this called?
questions.explanation: A favorable evaluation was offered in exchange for sexual favors.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Securing a crashed vehicle with cribbing, struts, or other supports so it cannot move, shift, or roll; it must be done to ensure the vehicle is stable before attempting to access a patient trapped inside.
questions.explanation: vehicle stabilization: Securing a crashed vehicle with cribbing, struts, or other supports so it cannot move, shift, or roll; it must be done to ensure the vehicle is stable before attempting to access a patient trapped inside.

questions.question: A firefighter breathes dust at a collapse where a patient later tests positive for tuberculosis. He is not sick, but he must be tested and followed. What term describes his situation?
questions.explanation: He had contact with airborne particles that could cause disease — an exposure requiring follow-up.

questions.question: In Dallas in 2014, ICU nurses Nina Pham and Amber Vinson were infected with Ebola after caring for patient Thomas Eric Duncan; Vinson had inserted catheters, drawn blood, and handled heavy body-fluid exposure. What does their infection demonstrate about PPE?
choices: PPE is unnecessary when the provider is experienced with the procedures being performed.
Gloves alone provide adequate protection against blood and body fluids.
For high-risk fluids, PPE must be complete and removed in the correct sequence — no shortcuts.
PPE can be removed in any order as long as handwashing happens afterward.
questions.explanation: The nurses were infected through direct contact with infectious body fluids, so complete PPE and correct removal sequence are essential.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Protective equipment that blocks exposure to a pathogen or a hazardous material.
questions.explanation: personal protective equipment: Protective equipment that blocks exposure to a pathogen or a hazardous material.

questions.question: The white-footed mouse is the principal reservoir host of Borrelia burgdorferi, the Lyme disease bacterium, in the northeastern United States. Larval blacklegged ticks acquire the bacterium by feeding on infected mice, then later feed on people. For a patient with suspected tick-borne illness, what should the exposure history include?
choices: Only adult tick bites, because larval ticks cannot carry the bacterium from the mouse host.
Where the host animals live, such as woods, leaf litter, and brush, because that is where the tick exposure happens.
Whether the patient was bitten directly by a mouse, since mice transmit Lyme to people themselves.
Time spent in open water and beaches, since Lyme risk is highest in aquatic environments.
questions.explanation: For tick-borne illness, exposure history should cover where the host animals live: woods, leaf litter, and brush.

questions.question: During CPR on a patient with tuberculosis, compressions and bag-mask ventilation push air out of the airway with each cycle. Why does the crew need airborne precautions?
questions.explanation: CPR is an airway manipulation that produces aerosols, as the definition itself names.

questions.question: Your crew is dispatched to a nursing home where 14 residents developed vomiting and diarrhea a day after the same catered lunch. The suspected route of spread is a contaminated meal. What type of transmission is this?
questions.explanation: Illness caused by an organism contaminating food is foodborne transmission.

questions.question: After three years of back-to-back traumatic calls with no break, a paramedic feels constantly exhausted, dreads every shift, and cannot sleep — yet there was no single bad call. What is this pattern called?
questions.explanation: The symptoms built up from prolonged, repeated stress over time rather than one incident.

questions.question: What does the term "substance abuse" mean?
choices: A stress disorder characterized by gradual lessening of compassion over time.
The body's ability to protect itself from acquiring a disease.

The misuse of drugs or alcohol by a provider, on or off duty, that endangers the provider, coworkers, and patients; among EMS personnel, its most serious consequence is substandard or inappropriate patient care.
The organism or individual that is attacked by the infecting agent.
questions.explanation: substance abuse: The misuse of drugs or alcohol by a provider, on or off duty, that endangers the provider, coworkers, and patients; among EMS personnel, its most serious consequence is substandard or inappropriate patient care.
